challenges.text: Our biggest German client is asking us to add an AI-driven product recommendation engine to their e-commerce platform; we have 18 months of transaction history across 340,000 SKUs but none of our current developers have the machine learning depth to build a production-grade model — we lost the last tender because a Polish competitor could show a working prototype.
challenges.detail: One of our largest German clients, a regional e-commerce distributor, has asked us to build a product recommendation engine that runs inside their existing platform. They have given us read access to 18 months of transaction records covering around 340,000 active SKUs, plus some basic customer segmentation data. The problem is that none of our current developers have built and deployed a machine learning model at this scale before. We ran a small experiment using an open-source collaborative filtering library and the results were not good enough to show the client. We lost an earlier tender on a similar brief because a competitor from Poland was able to demonstrate a working prototype in the pitch meeting — we could not. The client has given us roughly 18 months before they would consider moving the work elsewhere. We need someone who can help us design a model architecture that can actually go into production, train on the data we already have, and connect to our existing Node.js back end. We are also open to a transfer of knowledge so our own team can maintain and retrain the model going forward rather than being dependent on outside help indefinitely.

challenges.text: We onboard roughly four new EU clients a year, and every single one requires us to sign their own data processing agreement under GDPR; our lead developer is spending almost two weeks per contract just reviewing clauses, which is pulling him off billable work and we can't afford an in-house lawyer.
challenges.detail: Every new EU client we sign requires us to agree to their own data processing agreement before we can start work. The language in these contracts varies significantly — some are straightforward, some include clauses around sub-processor lists, audit rights, and data residency that need careful reading before we sign. Right now our lead developer, Marko Ilić, is the person who reviews all of them because he has the most experience with how our systems actually handle data. He estimates he spends close to two weeks of billable time per contract on this review, which at our project margins is genuinely painful. We have tried using a standard template from a Serbian IT industry association as a reference point, but clients do not accept our version — they want us to sign theirs. We cannot justify a full-time in-house lawyer for four contracts a year. We are looking for a practical way to speed up this review process and reduce the burden on our technical staff, whether that is a structured checklist, a clause-comparison tool, or a repeatable workflow that someone without a legal background can actually follow.

challenges.text: Our CI/CD pipeline runs full regression on every push and the test suite now takes 4.5 hours; developers are merging less often and bugs are slipping through because people skip the wait, so our defect escape rate to production has gone up from 2% to 9% over the last six months.
challenges.detail: Our test suite has grown alongside our client base and now takes about four and a half hours to run end to end. We run it on every push to the main branch via GitLab CI/CD on a self-managed runner cluster hosted on AWS. The tests themselves are a mix of Jest unit tests and Playwright end-to-end scenarios that were written over several years without much central coordination, so there is significant overlap between them. The practical result is that developers have started merging less frequently and in some cases are bypassing the full run by targeting only the subset of tests that cover their immediate change. Over the last six months our defect escape rate to production has climbed from around 2 percent to around 9 percent, and we have had two client-facing incidents that we attribute directly to this. We have tried parallelising some of the Playwright tests across multiple runner instances and brought the time down from about six hours, but four and a half hours is still too long to maintain good development habits. We need help thinking about how to restructure the suite — potentially through test selection, better parallelisation, or identifying and removing redundant coverage — without reducing actual confidence in what we ship.

challenges.text: Three Dutch clients want their dashboards to show carbon footprint per shipment in real time, but we have no in-house expertise on emission factor databases or lifecycle calculation standards — we are guessing at methodology and one client has already flagged that our numbers don't match their own consultant's figures.
challenges.detail: Three of our Dutch logistics clients have asked us to display carbon footprint figures per shipment on their operational dashboards. We built the basic display layer without difficulty, but the underlying calculation is where we are struggling. We do not have anyone on the team with a background in emissions accounting or lifecycle assessment, so we researched publicly available emission factor tables and built a calculation ourselves. One client then compared our figures against a report produced by their own sustainability consultant and found meaningful discrepancies — in one case our per-kilometre figure for road freight was around 30 percent lower than the consultant's. We do not know whether the gap is in the emission factor source, the allocation method, or somewhere in our load and distance logic. The clients are not asking for certified calculations, but they do need figures they can use in their own reporting without embarrassment. We need someone who understands the relevant calculation standards — particularly around freight transport — and can help us build a methodology that is defensible and consistent, and ideally point us toward the right data sources so we can maintain it ourselves as emission factor tables are updated.

companies.plans: Velago plans to grow its logistics client base in Germany and the Netherlands over the next two years, with a focus on clients who need ongoing platform development rather than one-off project work. We are also actively looking at adding data and analytics capability to our service offering so we can handle a wider range of client requirements in-house.
companies.rd_capacity: We have no dedicated research function, but two senior developers currently spend around 20 percent of their time on internal tooling and technical exploration between client projects.
companies.past_collaborations: Velago completed a small joint feasibility study in 2021 with the Faculty of Technical Sciences in Novi Sad on automated API documentation generation, which did not proceed beyond the prototype stage.

companies.name: Sentinel Byte preduzetnik
companies.about:
Sentinel Byte was started in 2021 by Dragan Kovačević and his son Nikola Kovačević in Subotica. Dragan spent over twenty years maintaining IT infrastructure for a regional logistics company before deciding to put that experience toward helping smaller organisations understand their actual security exposure. Nikola came in from a computer science background with hands-on experience in network scanning and web application testing. Together they built a six-person team that covers penetration testing, security audits, and basic security consulting for clients across northern Vojvodina.

Our clients are mostly small and medium businesses — accountancy firms, medical clinics, small manufacturers — and a handful of local municipalities who have formal obligations under Serbian information security regulations but limited in-house expertise to meet them. We do not sell fear. We run structured tests, document what we find in plain language, and sit with the client until they understand what each finding means for their daily operations.

What separates us from larger firms is geography and availability. We are based in Subotica, we know the local regulatory environment, and our clients can call Dragan or Nikola directly. Six people means no account managers and no hand-offs. Every engagement is run by someone who also wrote the test plan.
products: External and internal network penetration testing
Web application security audit
Security posture assessment for small municipalities
Post-audit remediation walkthrough session
Phishing simulation and basic staff awareness workshop
tech: Nmap and Nessus for network scanning
Burp Suite for web application testing

challenges.text: We run manual penetration tests that take our team about two weeks per engagement; clients are asking for continuous testing and retest after patches, but at our size we simply can't bill enough hours to make that sustainable — we need a way to automate at least the reconnaissance and vulnerability enumeration phases.
challenges.detail: A standard engagement for us runs about two weeks: a few days of reconnaissance and enumeration, then active testing, then a reporting phase. That rhythm works when a client wants a point-in-time audit once a year. The problem is that several clients — especially the two municipalities and a regional medical supply company — have started asking us to retest after they apply patches, and one of them mentioned they want something closer to monthly checks on their external attack surface. We simply do not have the hours to bill that at our current rates and stay profitable. We have tried writing Bash scripts to partially automate the initial scanning phase, and that saves maybe two hours per engagement, but it is fragile and hard to maintain. We need a more reliable pipeline that can run scheduled reconnaissance and vulnerability enumeration, flag changes since the last scan, and hand results to our testers in a structured format. If we could cut the first phase from four days to one, we could take on retest work without adding headcount. Budget for tooling or a development collaboration is limited — roughly 3,000 to 5,000 euros — but we are open to a research arrangement where the output is a working prototype.

challenges.text: Two municipalities hired us and then couldn't act on our findings because their IT staff didn't understand the remediation steps; we'd like a structured training programme we could sell alongside the audit, but writing curriculum and measuring knowledge retention is not something we know how to do.
challenges.detail: After finishing audits for two municipal clients, Opština Kanjiza and a second municipality we are not naming publicly, we delivered detailed reports and then watched nothing get fixed for three months. When we followed up, the honest answer from their IT coordinators was that the remediation steps read like a foreign language to them. We ran two informal afternoon sessions explaining the findings in plain terms, and that actually helped — one municipality patched four out of seven critical issues within a month afterward. So we know training works, but right now we deliver it informally and for free because we have no product to charge for. We would like to build a short structured programme — probably four to six modules — that we can sell as an add-on to any audit. The challenge is we do not know how to design curriculum properly, how to test whether people retained anything, or how to keep the material updated as the threat landscape changes. We have the technical content in our heads. We need help turning it into something repeatable and measurable. A good outcome would be a pilot programme we could test with one municipality client by the end of this year.

challenges.text: We've been trying for five months to register as a certified auditor under the Serbian Information Security Law so we can bid on public procurement contracts, but the paperwork at the Ministry keeps bouncing back for minor formal reasons and we don't know how to fix it.
challenges.detail: Serbian law on information security requires that organisations in certain sectors use certified auditors for their mandatory audits. That certification would open public procurement to us, which currently we cannot bid on at all. We applied to the Ministry five months ago and have had the application returned three times, each time with a short note citing a formal deficiency. The first return was about the formatting of an attached document. The second was about a reference number on a supporting form. The third cited an unclear clause about professional experience documentation. We have tried reading the relevant rulebook ourselves and consulting a general business lawyer in Subotica who was honest enough to say she does not know this specific regulatory area well. We are not looking for legal advice in the strict sense — we just need someone who has successfully navigated this specific process and can look at our application package and tell us concretely what is wrong. A good outcome is a submitted application that does not come back. We would like to resolve this within the next three months because there is a municipal procurement round opening in the autumn that we want to be eligible for.

companies.plans: Over the next twelve months we want to add one junior tester and move at least part of our reconnaissance workflow onto an automated platform so we can offer continuous monitoring as a service. We are also looking to formalise our training offering into a product we can price and repeat.
companies.rd_capacity: Nikola Kovačević can dedicate roughly two days per week to a collaborative development project, primarily on tooling and automation topics.
companies.past_collaborations: Informal technical consultation with a Subotica-based IT services firm, Netlogika d.o.o., during a joint client engagement in 2023; no formal research or university collaborations to date.

companies.name: Pannonia Osiguranje-Tech a.d.
companies.sector: Insurtech — usage-based motor and property insurance
companies.about: Pannonia Osiguranje-Tech a.d. was established in 2009 in Subotica, when a small group of insurance professionals decided that the Vojvodina market deserved a carrier built around data rather than paperwork. We started with straightforward motor and household policies for private customers in the northern Serbia corridor, then spent the following decade quietly replacing manual underwriting steps with sensor-driven and rules-based processes. Today our 187 staff serve roughly 41,000 active policyholders across Serbia, Bosnia-Herzegovina and North Macedonia, with a Romanian branch application under review. Our motor book covers private cars, light commercial vehicles and agricultural machinery; our property book covers urban apartments, rural households and, increasingly, farm buildings and standing crops in the Vojvodina plains. What sets us apart is the combination of a regional insurer's knowledge of local claim patterns with the tooling usually found in larger markets: telematics hardware fitted in about 9,400 vehicles, a smart-home sensor kit sold under our own label, and a pricing function that reruns rating factors every quarter rather than every renewal cycle. Our leadership team is led by Chief Executive Mirela Bogdanović and Chief Actuary Dragan Fekete, supported by product, claims and technology heads based in Subotica and a small Belgrade office.

Smart-home property insurance with connected smoke, flood and motion sensors
Agricultural property insurance for farm buildings and standing crops

challenges.text: Our telematics black-box records speed, braking and cornering, but we still price everyone in the same age-vehicle bracket the same way — we need a model that actually translates raw trip events into a per-driver risk score we can price off.
challenges.detail: Every trip our black-box records produces a stream of events — speed samples every two seconds, hard-brake flags, sharp-cornering flags, night-driving flags. We store all of it in our PostgreSQL warehouse, so the raw material is there: roughly 380 million trip-event rows covering the last four years and about 9,400 active devices. The problem is that our pricing team of four has never had the time or the specific background to turn those rows into something the rating engine can use. Right now we group drivers only by age band and vehicle category, which means a cautious 24-year-old pays the same as an aggressive one. We tried building a simple points-based score in-house last year but the loss ratio on the telematics segment barely moved. What we want is a scoring method that takes the raw events, accounts for trip length and road type as far as we can infer it, and outputs a single per-driver number we can map directly onto a loading or discount. Our target is to have something running in the rating engine before the next annual product filing, which is due in the first quarter of 2026. Budget for outside help is modest but real — we can provide full access to the anonymised trip data under a data-processing agreement.

challenges.text: Property claims for hail damage on Vojvodina farms are costing us about 18% more per claim than our pricing assumed; we believe we're underestimating exposure because we don't know how to map hail intensity at field level.
challenges.detail: Hail claims on Vojvodina farm property have been running about 18% above our loss assumption for the past three summers. Our current approach is to rate by municipality and apply a single hail loading per municipality, but Vojvodina hailstorms are narrow and fast-moving — a storm can devastate one village and leave the farm two kilometres away untouched. We do receive daily gridded weather data from MeteoVoj d.o.o. at a five-kilometre resolution, but we have not been able to link that data reliably to individual policy locations because a large share of our farm addresses are stored only at the settlement level, not as coordinates. We have tried overlaying the MeteoVoj grid manually in QGIS for the worst claim years, and the patterns look promising, but turning that into something that feeds the pricing model automatically is beyond what our team can do alone. A good outcome would be a method that takes our policy locations, matches them to hail intensity estimates at field level, and tells us which parts of our portfolio are priced too low. We have three full claim years with geo-tagged loss data for about 1,200 farm policies to work with.

challenges.text: We're trying to enter the Romanian market but the local regulator is asking for a Solvency II internal model validation report and we don't have the actuarial staff to produce one — our pricing team has four people.
challenges.detail: We submitted our Romanian branch application in late 2023 and the regulator has come back asking for an internal model validation report under Solvency II. This was not unexpected, but we underestimated how much work it involves. Our pricing team is four actuaries, two of whom joined in the last eighteen months and are still working toward their full fellowship exams. The remaining two are fully occupied with Serbia and Bosnia product filings. We have a standard formula model running for our Serbian regulatory returns, so we have the capital model concept — the gap is the formal validation documentation, the backtesting of loss distributions and the narrative that explains why the model is appropriate for our business mix. The Romanian portfolio we are proposing is small: private motor and urban apartment property only, capped at 5,000 policies in year one. We are not looking for someone to rebuild our model; we need someone who understands the Solvency II validation framework and can work with our two senior actuaries to produce a report the regulator will accept. We are targeting submission by October 2025, so the work would need to start by May at the latest.

companies.plans: Pannonia Osiguranje-Tech aims to complete its Romanian market entry by the end of 2025 and begin selling telematics motor policies there by mid-2026. Over the same period, the company plans to replace its on-premise Guidewire instance with a cloud-hosted version and extend the smart-home sensor kit to rental-property landlords.
companies.rd_capacity: The company has no dedicated research unit; applied development work is carried out by a four-person pricing team and a six-person IT team who split their time between operational support and new product build.
companies.past_collaborations: Pannonia Osiguranje-Tech worked with Fakultet tehničkih nauka in Novi Sad on a small ERASMUS+ project in 2021 to prototype a flood-risk mapping tool for the Sava floodplain, which was completed but not yet integrated into the pricing system.

companies.name: Kvantor Inženjering d.o.o.
companies.sector: Custom software and IT services for EU clients
companies.about: Kvantor Inženjering d.o.o. was founded in Novi Sad in 1997 by a small group of engineers who had spent the previous decade building industrial control software for domestic factories. When Serbian manufacturers began integrating with European supply chains, we shifted our focus to ERP integration and reporting services for mid-market manufacturers in Germany, Austria and the Netherlands. Today we employ 220 people across our Novi Sad headquarters and a small coordination office in Vienna. Our clients are production companies with between 150 and 2,000 employees who need reliable data infrastructure but cannot justify the overhead of a large in-house IT department. We handle ERP integration, business intelligence dashboards, and managed infrastructure — work that is unglamorous but critical. What keeps clients with us is consistency: our average client relationship runs seven years, and the same engineers who onboarded a client typically continue to support them. We are not a consultancy that sells transformation roadmaps; we build and operate systems. Our technical staff average nine years of industry experience. We are headquartered at Novi Sad Science and Technology Park, which gives us access to applied research contacts we use when a problem outgrows standard tooling.

Business intelligence dashboards and monthly reporting pipelines
Managed infrastructure hosting with EU data-residency options

Staff augmentation for manufacturing IT projects

challenges.text: We maintain BI dashboards for nine German manufacturing clients and each month we spend roughly 400 analyst-hours cleaning and reconciling data from SAP, legacy MES systems and spreadsheets before any report can go out — we need to automate that pipeline but the schemas change with every client upgrade.
challenges.detail: We run monthly BI reporting for nine German manufacturing clients. Every report cycle starts the same way: our analysts pull data from each client's SAP system, one or two legacy MES platforms, and a collection of Excel files that shop-floor supervisors maintain outside any formal system. Reconciling all of that takes roughly 400 analyst-hours per month across the team. The core problem is that client schemas change constantly — an SAP upgrade, a new production line, a change in how a plant codes its cost centers — and our existing ETL scripts break without warning. We have tried building more defensive pipelines in Airflow with schema-validation steps, and that caught some breakage earlier, but it still requires a human to diagnose and fix each mismatch. We have the raw data, we have access to client systems, and we have two senior data engineers who understand the domain well. What we need is a way to detect schema drift automatically and adapt mappings without full manual rewrites each time. A good result would be cutting that 400-hour monthly burden by at least half while keeping report accuracy at current levels.

challenges.text: A Dutch client processes personal data of 80,000 customers through our hosted platform; after their internal audit flagged a gap in our data-residency documentation, we've been asked to achieve ISO 27001 certification within nine months or lose the contract, and we've never done a formal ISMS implementation.
challenges.detail: One of our Dutch clients, a mid-sized packaging manufacturer, runs their customer management and order processing through a platform we host on Azure in the Amsterdam region. Their internal audit team reviewed our data-handling documentation earlier this year and found that our records on data residency, access controls and incident response procedures were not formalized to a standard they could show to their own regulators. They have given us nine months to achieve ISO 27001 certification or they will move the platform in-house. That contract represents roughly 12 percent of our annual revenue. We have never implemented a formal Information Security Management System. We understand the technical controls well enough — we already run encryption at rest, role-based access and regular backups — but we have no documented risk register, no formal asset inventory, no supplier assessment process, and no internal audit cycle. We have one IT security officer on staff who handles day-to-day access management but has not led a certification project. Budget for external support is available but not unlimited. A good outcome is certification within the deadline with processes our team can actually maintain afterward.

challenges.text: Our junior consultants take on average 11 months to reach billable productivity; we lose about €60k per head in that ramp period and attrition at month 14 means we rarely recoup it.
challenges.detail: We hire junior consultants and developers from universities in Novi Sad and Belgrade every year. On paper this is straightforward: we take graduates, train them on SAP integration, our internal tooling and client communication standards, and after a ramp period they carry billable work. In practice the ramp takes an average of eleven months before someone is generating enough billable output to cover their cost. We have calculated that we absorb roughly sixty thousand euros per head during that period in salary, supervisor time and client relationship risk. The bigger problem is that a meaningful share of those staff leave around month fourteen — right after they have become productive — typically for a Western European employer or a larger tech company. So we carry the full ramp cost and rarely get more than a few months of return. We have tried a structured mentoring program and a revised onboarding curriculum, which shortened some early ramp stages, but has not moved the overall number much. We want to understand whether the bottleneck is curriculum design, the way we assign early project work, or something else, and then build a training approach that is repeatable and measurable.

challenges.text: Three Austrian clients asked us to add natural-language querying to their BI dashboards so non-technical managers can ask questions in German and get correct SQL-backed charts; our test with an off-the-shelf LLM produced wrong aggregations in roughly 40% of finance queries.
challenges.detail: Three of our Austrian manufacturing clients want their managers to be able to type a question in plain German — something like 'what was our rejection rate on line three last quarter compared to the previous year' — and get back a correct chart without involving an analyst. We ran a pilot using an off-the-shelf large language model connected to one client's SQL database. The model produced plausible-looking queries, but when we checked the outputs against manually prepared reports, roughly forty percent of finance-related questions returned wrong aggregations — incorrect groupings, missing filters, misunderstood date ranges. The problem is not the language understanding; the model handles German phrasing reasonably well. The problem is that our clients' data models are complex and underdocumented, and the model has no reliable way to know which tables and columns actually mean what the business user intends. We have the schemas, some data dictionaries of varying quality, and samples of analyst-written queries that we know are correct. We need an approach that uses that existing material to constrain query generation reliably. A good outcome is a system where finance managers can run routine queries without analyst involvement and the error rate on those queries is below five percent.

companies.plans: Over the next two years Kvantor plans to deepen its presence in the Austrian market by adding two dedicated account managers and expanding managed infrastructure capacity in the Frankfurt region. We are also evaluating whether to build a formal data engineering practice as a standalone service line rather than treating it as part of ERP delivery.
companies.rd_capacity: We can allocate two senior engineers and one data analyst for up to six months on a defined research collaboration, provided deliverables connect directly to a client-facing product or process.
companies.past_collaborations: We completed a two-year applied project with a software engineering group at a regional technical faculty between 2019 and 2021, focused on automated test generation for ERP integration scripts, which resulted in a testing framework we still use internally.

companies.name: Kristal Voda preduzetnik
companies.sector: Water quality testing and on-site treatment equipment for food industry
companies.about: Kristal Voda was founded in 2011 by Miroslav Đurić, a water-treatment technician who spent a decade servicing municipal waterworks before deciding to focus on the food and beverage sector. Based in Zrenjanin, we supply and maintain water softeners, UV disinfection units, and portable water-quality testing kits to bakeries, dairies, and beverage producers across central and southern Vojvodina. Our clients range from small family bakeries to mid-sized dairy operations processing several thousand litres of milk per day. What sets us apart is straightforward: we do the installation, the maintenance, and the troubleshooting ourselves. There is no call centre and no outsourced service team. When something goes wrong at a dairy in Kikinda at six in the morning, Miroslav or one of our technicians picks up the phone. Our nine-person team includes four field technicians, two sales and client-support staff, a part-time lab assistant, an administrator, and Miroslav himself. We source equipment from established European manufacturers and carry our own stock of consumables — resins, UV lamps, test-kit reagents — so clients rarely wait more than a day for a replacement part. We are not the cheapest option in the region, but our clients value the fact that one company handles the full chain from water analysis through equipment supply to ongoing service.

UV disinfection units for inlet water and CIP rinse water

challenges.text: Three of our dairy clients have reported a sulphur smell in their process water after we installed new ion-exchange softeners; we've flushed and regenerated the resins but the problem reappears within two weeks and one client has threatened to cancel.
challenges.detail: About eight months ago we fitted three dairy clients with new ion-exchange softeners from a batch we sourced from a different supplier than usual. Within a few weeks all three reported a sulphur or rotten-egg smell in their process water. We flushed the resin beds thoroughly and ran full regeneration cycles with clean brine, and the smell went away. But it came back within ten to fourteen days each time. We tested the inlet water before the softeners — no sulphur detectable. We also checked the brine we use for regeneration and it looks clean. Our best guess is that something in the new resin batch is either harbouring sulphate-reducing bacteria or releasing a sulphur compound as it degrades, but we cannot pin it down. One of the three clients, a dairy in Novi Bečej producing around 4,000 litres of processed milk per day, has told us they will cancel their maintenance contract if we cannot fix this by autumn. We have the original resin batch documentation and some water samples in our Zrenjanin storage. We do not have a lab of our own. We need someone who can analyse the resin and the water, tell us what is happening chemically or microbiologically, and help us put a lasting fix in place.

challenges.text: Our portable turbidity and nitrate test kits give inconsistent readings in hard water above 450 mg/L CaCO₃; we calibrate with distilled water but field samples from Banat wells are much harder and the kits weren't designed for that matrix.
challenges.detail: Our portable test kits for turbidity and nitrate were specified for water up to about 300 mg/L CaCO₃ hardness, which covers most of our clients. The problem is that several Banat well sources we now work with sit well above 450 mg/L CaCO₃, sometimes reaching 550 mg/L. When our technicians use the kits on those field samples, the readings jump around — we get turbidity values 20 to 30 percent higher than what a reference lab returns for the same sample, and nitrate readings are sometimes low by a similar margin. We have tried calibrating with distilled water and with tap water from Zrenjanin, but neither matches the sample matrix. We do not have the budget to send every field sample to an external lab; the whole point of the kits is fast, on-site results that clients can see during a visit. We would like to understand whether a simple matrix-matched calibration standard could fix this, whether there is a correction factor we can apply, or whether the chemistry of the kits needs to be adjusted. A practical, field-usable solution is what matters — our technicians are not chemists and any fix needs to work with handheld equipment.

companies.plans: Over the next two years we want to add dissolved-oxygen and pH monitoring to our service offering, targeting the beverage sector where those parameters matter for fermentation water. We are also considering a small in-house testing bench so we can run basic resin and water analyses without relying entirely on external labs.
companies.rd_capacity: We have no dedicated R&D staff, but Miroslav and our part-time lab assistant can contribute time to testing and field trials if given clear protocols.
companies.past_collaborations: None formal; we have informally consulted with the water-supply company Vodovod Zrenjanin on local groundwater chemistry on two occasions.

companies.name: Paleta Kreativa preduzetnik
companies.sector: Marketing tech, media and creative studios
companies.about: Paleta Kreativa started in 2019 when Erzsébet and Tamás Varga decided that small shops and guesthouses in Vojvodina deserved the same quality of social media content as big-city brands. Working first from their kitchen table in Subotica, they built a small team of six people who all grew up switching between Serbian and Hungarian before breakfast. Today we manage 34 active accounts for local retailers, restaurants, and tourism operators stretching from Subotica down through Senta and across the border into southern Hungary. Every piece of content we produce — a short video of a paprika harvest, a reel for a family-run thermal spa, a product post for a shoe shop on Korzo — goes through a bilingual review before it goes live. We are not a large agency. We do not take on clients outside our region, and we think that focus is exactly what our clients are paying for. Our team of six handles everything from script writing and filming to scheduling and comment moderation. Tamás leads production, Erzsébet handles client relationships, and the rest of the team are community managers and one part-time editor. We are still family-run, still based in Subotica, and still small enough that we know every client by name.

Bilingual community management in Serbian and Hungarian
Content calendar planning and scheduling

challenges.text: We manage 34 client accounts in both Serbian and Hungarian and our community managers keep making grammar mistakes when they switch languages mid-day; one client in Senta publicly complained about a post, and we need some kind of assisted writing or review tool that handles both languages.
challenges.detail: We post in both Serbian and Hungarian every single day across 34 accounts. Our community managers are fluent in both languages but switching back and forth under time pressure leads to slip-ups — a Serbian verb form landing in a Hungarian caption, or a dative ending used where it shouldn't be. One client in Senta, a tourism guesthouse, publicly posted a screenshot of a caption error on their own page, which was embarrassing for everyone. We have tried a basic proofreading checklist and we ask team members to review each other's work, but with the volume we handle, that review step often gets skipped when things are busy. We have no tool that flags language-mixing errors for these two specific languages together. A spell-checker for one language just ignores text written in the other. What we need is something lightweight — ideally a browser extension or a simple web form — that a community manager can paste text into, select the target language, and get flagged corrections back in under a minute. We are not looking for a full translation engine. We have a small monthly software budget of around 80 to 120 euros, and the tool needs to work without heavy training.

challenges.text: Short-form video for Hungarian tourism clients performs very differently depending on whether we post at 11:00 or 19:00, but we have no reliable model for optimal posting time per audience segment; we're leaving engagement on the table.
challenges.detail: We have noticed for a while that posting times make a real difference for our tourism clients in particular. A reel we post at 11:00 for a thermal spa page in southern Hungary might get 40 interactions, but the same quality reel posted at 19:00 gets 180. The problem is we have no model that tells us which time slot to use for which audience. Meta Business Suite gives us some general audience activity data but it is averaged across all days and does not separate local Serbian-speaking followers from Hungarian-speaking ones, which for several of our cross-border clients is a meaningful difference. We have been keeping a manual log in a Google Sheet for about eight months — post time, day of week, language of caption, engagement count — across roughly 12 of our most active accounts. That is about 900 rows of data now. We have tried reading patterns by eye but we are not analysts and it is not reliable. What we want is a simple model or even a clear lookup table that tells us, for a given account type and language segment, the best two or three posting windows per day. We are not expecting a live dashboard. A working recommendation we can apply to our scheduling workflow would be enough.

challenges.text: We need to buy a gimbal rig and a second mirrorless camera body to keep up with demand, but the banks want two full years of financial statements and we only have four; the leasing options we found have interest rates above 12 %.
challenges.detail: Client demand for on-location video has grown faster than our equipment can handle. We currently own one Sony mirrorless body and a single-axis gimbal that is starting to show wear. When two clients book shoots on the same day — which now happens about twice a month — we have to decline one or reschedule, which costs us goodwill and sometimes the booking entirely. We priced a second camera body and a proper three-axis gimbal rig together at roughly 2,200 euros. We approached two banks for a small business loan and both asked for two years of financial statements minimum; we have four years of records so that was not the obstacle, but both offers came back above 12 percent annual interest, which we cannot absorb on equipment that depreciates. Leasing options we found through a local broker were similar or worse. We have not applied for any EU or national grant instruments yet because we are not sure which ones apply to a preduzetnik of our size. We need the equipment within the next three to four months to cover the summer tourism season, which is our highest-revenue period.

companies.plans: Paleta Kreativa plans to expand its client base to ten additional tourism operators in the Palić and Bečej areas by the end of 2025. We are also exploring a small subscription package for Hungarian-diaspora food and craft businesses that sell online.
companies.rd_capacity: We can contribute real bilingual posting data, client account access for testing, and hands-on feedback from active community managers, but we have no in-house developer or data analyst.
companies.past_collaborations: We completed a short paid project in 2023 with Vizuál Stúdió Kft., a small graphic design firm in Szeged, to co-produce a branded content series for a cross-border cycling tourism client.

companies.name: TloCare d.o.o.
companies.about:
TloCare d.o.o. osnovan je 2013. godine u Novom Sadu sa jednom idejom: da kooperativama i agro-input trgovcima u Vojvodini pruži jasnu sliku o tome šta se dešava ispod površine njihovih njiva. Počeli smo sa dva agrohemičara, terenskim vozilom i dogovorom sa jednim regionalnim laboratorijem. Danas nas je dvadeset dvoje i radimo sa više od četrdeset kooperativa i distributivnih centara od Subotice do Zrenjanina.

Naša osnovna usluga je uzorkovanje zemljišta po mreži, laboratorijska analiza i dostava nutrientnih mapa kroz naš web portal koji su stranicu dizajnirali sami naši klijenti — bez nepotrebnih funkcija, samo ono što agronomu treba kada stigne s polja. Rezultati koje klijent vidi odnose se na pH, fosfor, kalijum, humus i potrebu za kalcifikacijom, uz preporuku za đubrenje po parcelama.

Ne prodajemo softver kao proizvod. Nudimo uslugu od uzorkovanja do preporuke, i ostajemo uz klijenta tokom sezone. Naš tim čine agrohemičari, jedan GIS specijalista i dva programera koji održavaju portal. Terenska ekipa poznaje specifičnosti vojvođanskih serija zemljišta, posebno parcela uz Tisu gde se hidromorfna i aluvijalna tla smenjuju na kratkim rastojanjima.

Razlikujemo se po tome što ne tražimo od klijenta da uči novi sistem — mi donosimo podatke njemu u format koji već razume.

challenges.text: We do traditional grid sampling at one point per 4 hectares but clients with highly variable soils — especially those with old floodplain deposits near the Tisa — say our maps miss the pockets of salinity that are killing their sunflower establishment, and we can't afford to sample more densely.
challenges.detail: Radimo grid uzorkovanje sa jednom tačkom na četiri hektara, što je standard koji funkcioniše na uniformnim parcelama centralnog Banata. Ali klijenti čije su njive uz Tisu — na primer kooperativa 'Ravnica Agro' iz Novog Bečeja — stalno nam javljaju da im suncokret propadne na delovima parcele koji na mapi izgledaju dobro. Kada smo naknadno gušće uzorkovali nekoliko tih parcela, videli smo da slani džepovi postoje na površini od svega 0,3 do 0,8 hektara i da ih naša standardna mreža preskače. Problem je što gušće uzorkovanje znači više terena, više laboratorijskih troškova i duži rok isporuke — a cena usluge nam već pritiska granicu prihvatljivosti za klijenta. Probali smo da koristimo satelitske NDVI snimke kao vodič za adaptivno uzorkovanje, ali nismo imali dobre rezultate jer se salinitet ne vidi jasno na vegetacionim indeksima u ranom proleću. Imamo GPS koordinate svih dosadašnjih uzoraka i laboratorijske rezultate za oko 18.000 tačaka iz poslednjih deset godina. Dobar ishod bi bio da možemo da predvidimo gde su varijabilne zone pre nego što pošaljemo terenska ekipa, i da gušće uzorkujemo samo tamo gde je potrebno.

challenges.text: Our lab sends us pH, P, K, and humus results as PDF scans from three different partner laboratories — each with its own column format — and our team re-types 600 to 800 results per week into our database, which is error-prone and takes two full-time staff.
challenges.detail: Sarađujemo sa tri laboratorije — 'AgroLab Subotica', 'Tla-Hem Kikinda' i jednom privatnom laboratorijom u Sremskoj Mitrovici — i svaka nam šalje rezultate kao PDF scan, nekad i kao fotografiju dokumenta. Formati su različiti: jedna laboratorija stavlja pH pre fosfora, druga ima kalijum u meq/100g umesto mg/100g, treća spoji rezultate za više parcela u jednu tabelu bez jasnog razdvajanja redova. Naš tim provodi dva radna dana nedeljno samo na preucavanju i preucavanju unošenju podataka. Napravili smo Excel šablon i zamolili laboratorije da ga koriste, ali to nije zaživelo jer svaka ima sopstveni laboratorijski informacioni sistem koji generiše izveštaj automatski. Pokušali smo sa jednim komercijalnim OCR alatom, ali tačnost nije bila zadovoljavajuća — greška na numeričkim vrednostima je bila oko 4%, što je previše za agronomske preporuke. Imamo arhivu od oko 40.000 skeniranih PDF-ova od 2013. godine. Dobar ishod je sistem koji čita PDF bez ručnog posredovanja sa greškom ispod 0,5% i koji nas obavesti kada nešto ne može da pročita, umesto da tiho pogreši.

challenges.text: We want to add a liming recommendation engine that accounts for the buffer capacity of the specific soil type, not just the pH reading, but our team has chemistry backgrounds and we don't have the agronomy depth to model this properly for Vojvodina soil series.
challenges.detail: Trenutno preporučujemo količinu krečnjaka na osnovu izmerjenog pH i jednostavne tabele koju smo preuzeli iz jednog starijeg vojvođanskog priručnika. Problem je što peskovito-ilovasta tla u ritovima i teška glinovita tla na lesnoj terasi reaguju sasvim drugačije na iste doze krečnjaka — puferska sposobnost im se drastično razlikuje — i klijenti nam to govore godinama. Agronomi sa kojima smo razgovarali pominju Schöfield-ovu metodu i SMP pufer test, ali mi nemamo kapacitet da sami razvijemo model koji bi to primenio na konkretne serije zemljišta u Vojvodini. Naš tim su agrohemičari koji dobro razumeju analitiku, ali modelovanje puferske sposobnosti po tipovima tla zahteva agronomsku i pedološku dubinu koju trenutno nemamo. Imali bismo interes da izgradimo kalkulator koji uzima pH, teksturu i humus kao ulaz i vraća preporučenu dozu CaCO3 prilagođenu tipu tla. Raspolažemo podacima o parcelama za koje imamo i višegodišnja merenja, što bi moglo da posluži za validaciju modela. Rok koji nam odgovara je do sledeće prolećne sezone.

companies.plans: U naredne dve godine planiramo da uvedemo bar jednu vrstu terenskog senzorskog merenja (elektrokonduktivitet ili blisku infracrvenu spektroskopiju) kako bismo ponudili gušće prostorno pokriće bez proporcionalnog rasta troškova uzorkovanja. Takođe razmatramo proširenje portala na modularni sistem preporuka koji kooperative mogu da dele sa svojim članovima direktno.
companies.rd_capacity: Imamo dva programera i jednog GIS specijalista koji mogu da odvoje do trećine radnog vremena za razvoj novih funkcija, uz povremenu podršku terenske ekipe za testiranje u polju.
companies.past_collaborations: 2019. godine učestvovali smo u kratkom pilot projektu sa institutom 'Vojvodina Agro Centar' iz Sombora na temu optimizacije gustine uzorkovanja, ali saradnja nije formalizovana i nije objavljen zajednički rezultat.

companies.name: DriveLogic Vojvodina d.o.o.
companies.about:
DriveLogic Vojvodina d.o.o. was founded in 2004 by Miroslav Vučić, a mechanical and electronics engineer who spent fifteen years at a German Tier-1 supplier, and his son Andrej Vučić, who joined after finishing his electrical engineering degree in Novi Sad. The two of them started with three workstations in a rented room and a single contract to port BSW modules for a mid-size European passenger car program. Twenty years later we are a team of twenty-seven engineers, all based in Novi Sad, and we have delivered software integration work on more than forty OEM projects.

We focus entirely on AUTOSAR-based embedded software: configuration, integration, and V-cycle testing for powertrain, body and chassis ECUs. We do not build hardware, we do not sell IP, and we do not resell tools. Customers come to us because we do one thing and we do it carefully. Our engineers work directly inside the customer's development environment, using their toolchains and following their process rules.

Our main customers are Tier-1 and Tier-2 suppliers delivering ECUs to European OEMs. We have worked with companies such as Hartfeld Automotive Systems (Germany), Rennova Electronics (Czech Republic) and Balkon Drive Solutions (Slovakia). Most contracts run between six and twenty-four months.

What keeps customers coming back is straightforward: we document everything, we flag problems early, and we do not hide schedule risk.

V-cycle test planning, execution and coverage reporting for ECU software
CAN, LIN and Ethernet communication stack integration and validation

challenges.text: We manually generate around 3,200 AUTOSAR software component configuration files per project and it takes two engineers three weeks; one of our competitors apparently automated this and turned around the same job in four days — at current rates we are losing bids on price.
challenges.detail: Every new project hands us a System Extract from the customer and we then have to produce AUTOSAR SWC configuration files — port definitions, inter-runnable variables, timing constraints, the lot — by hand inside DaVinci Configurator. On the last two projects we counted roughly 3,200 files each time. Two senior engineers spend three weeks doing nothing else. We have tried building Excel-based templates to speed up the repetitive parts, and that helped a little, but the real problem is that the mapping logic between the System Extract and the final ARXML is still done by a person reading a document and typing. We heard from a contact at a Romanian company that they built something — probably a script or a generator layer on top of the tool API — that brings the same volume of work down to four days. We do not know the details. We have the DaVinci API documentation and we have two engineers who write Python, but nobody has had time to build the tooling properly. We are losing price-sensitive bids. A good outcome is a generation process that gets us from a clean System Extract to a reviewable first-draft configuration set in under one working day, with engineers only doing review and exception handling.

challenges.text: Our test coverage reports show 87% branch coverage but we keep finding integration bugs in the CAN communication stack after delivery; we suspect the problem is at the boundary between components from different suppliers but we have no systematic way to find those interaction faults before shipping.
challenges.detail: Our LDRA reports consistently show 87–89% branch coverage before we ship, which satisfies the contract threshold. But in the last four delivered projects, three of them came back with CAN communication faults found during customer integration testing. In each case the fault was at a boundary: one SWC from us, one SWC or COM configuration from a different supplier, both conforming to spec individually but producing unexpected behaviour when connected. We have tried adding integration test cases that exercise the COM layer explicitly, but we write those tests based on our own reading of the interface specification, so we tend to test what we already think is correct. We do not have a systematic way to generate tests that specifically target the assumptions each component makes about what the other will send. We have full access to the ARXML descriptions of all components in the project, the COM configuration, and the CANoe environment. What we need is a method — or tooling — that reads those descriptions and generates test scenarios aimed specifically at the interface contracts between components from different sources. Budget is not fixed but we would not start something that cost more than €40,000 in the first phase.

challenges.text: Three of our five engineers who do ECU flashing and diagnostic tooling learned on the job and have no formal training in UDS or OBD-II protocol internals; last year two of them left for a bigger company in Novi Sad within 18 months of joining and we had to restart their replacements from scratch — the training cost alone was over €25,000 each time.
challenges.detail: Five engineers handle ECU flashing and diagnostic work. Three of them learned by sitting next to a more experienced colleague and reading our internal cheat sheets. They can operate the tools but when something unusual comes up — a NRC they have not seen, a timing issue during a diagnostic session, a service routine behaving differently on a different ECU variant — they escalate to Andrej or to our one engineer who has formal protocol training, and that creates a bottleneck. The deeper problem is retention. In the last two years we lost two of those five engineers to a larger company in Novi Sad that offered higher salaries. Each time we had to hire a replacement and start from scratch. We calculated the internal training cost each time at just over €25,000, and that does not count the three to four months of reduced output while the new person gets up to speed. We have tried writing better internal documentation and we ran one informal workshop, but it was not systematic. We want something that a new hire can work through at their own pace and that tests their understanding before they touch a real vehicle. A structured, self-contained training path for UDS and OBD-II internals, ideally with practical exercises on simulated ECUs, would let us onboard faster and reduce how much senior engineer time gets burned on repeated explanations.

companies.plans: DriveLogic Vojvodina plans to add a second delivery team by end of 2026 so we can run two large OEM projects in parallel without resource conflicts. We are also evaluating whether to extend our service scope to cover AUTOSAR Adaptive on high-performance compute platforms, which several of our existing customers are beginning to ask about.
companies.rd_capacity: We can dedicate one senior engineer part-time (roughly 40% of their working week) to a collaborative development or research activity, provided it is directly tied to tools or methods we will use in active projects.
companies.past_collaborations: We worked informally with a controls research group at a technical institute in Subotica around 2019 on a model-based calibration study, but the output was not published and there was no formal agreement.

companies.name: BrzaPošta Logistics d.o.o.
companies.about:
BrzaPošta Logistics d.o.o. was founded in 2011 by Miroslav Đurić and Tamara Vuković, two former freight-forwarding coordinators who saw that small Serbian online retailers had no reliable way to get parcels to customers the next morning. We started with four vans and a rented garage in Futog. Today we operate 34 vehicles, a 2,400 square-metre sorting hub located just off the Novi Sad bypass near the Science and Technology Park, and a team of 87 people covering every postal code in Vojvodina plus a cross-border corridor into southern Hungary through our partner carrier KelInfo Szállítás Kft.

Our clients are mostly online retailers — fashion, electronics, pet supplies, home goods — ranging from two-person startups to regional warehouse operations moving a few hundred parcels a day. We also handle fulfilment storage for six clients who prefer not to manage their own warehouses.

What separates us from national carriers is local knowledge and direct accountability. Our dispatchers know Novi Sad street by street. When something goes wrong, clients reach a real person, not a call-centre script. We are not the cheapest option and we do not pretend to be; we compete on reliability and on actually delivering within the promised window. Our current on-time rate across standard shipments is 94.2%, measured against confirmed delivery timestamps.

Same-day express delivery within Novi Sad city limits
