challenges.text: Our voltage-regulation device works well in steady state but when it encounters high-frequency switching transients from nearby industrial variable-speed drives, it trips on overcurrent about once a week per installation — we have oscilloscope captures but no model that predicts when this will happen.
challenges.detail: Naš VR-400 uređaj radi pouzdano u normalnim uslovima, ali kada je u blizini industrijska instalacija s frekventnim regulatorima brzine motora, dolazi do kratkih naponskih prekoračenja koja aktiviraju zaštitu od prestruje. To se dešava otprilike jednom nedeljno po lokaciji, uvek u toku rada teških mašina. Imamo osciloskopske snimke dvadesetak takvih događaja — vidimo šiljke amplitude do 1,4 pu u trajanju od nekoliko mikrosekundi, ali nismo uspeli da odredimo koji parametri tačno dovode do isključivanja. Pokušali smo da ručno podesimo pragove zaštite, što je smanjilo broj isključivanja, ali povećalo rizik od oštećenja opreme. Nemamo fizički model koji bi unapred rekao kada je situacija kritična. Trebalo bi nam nešto između čistog elektromagnetnog modeliranja i analize vremenskih serija iz naših snimaka — neko ko može da poveže te dve stvari i da nam da kriterijum koji možemo ugraditi u firmware. Rok je realan: sledeća serija VR-400 uređaja ide u proizvodnju za šest meseci.

challenges.text: We want to offer a real-time volt-VAR optimisation service across a feeder with 200+ nodes, but our current solver takes 4–6 minutes on a standard server, which is too slow to respond to the 5-minute SCADA update cycle the operators use.
challenges.detail: Nudimo operatorima uslugu optimizacije napona i reaktivne snage duž celog feedera. Problem je što naš trenutni solver, koji radi na standardnom serveru s 16 jezgara, treba četiri do šest minuta da izračuna optimalne setpoint vrednosti za mrežu s više od 200 čvorova. Operatori dobijaju podatke od SCADA sistema svakih pet minuta, što znači da naš rezultat kasni za situacijom na terenu. Probali smo da smanjimo granularnost modela, ali to pogoršava tačnost dovoljno da operatori primete razliku i izgube poverenje u preporuke. Koristimo sopstveni solver baziran na relaksiranoj semidefinitnoj formulaciji. Nismo sigurni da li je usko grlo u samom algoritmu, u načinu na koji učitavamo topologiju mreže, ili u nečem drugom. Nije nam potrebna savršena teorijska rešenost — potrebno je da ciklus bude kraći od tri minuta na istom hardveru, sa tačnošću koja nije lošija od sadašnje.

challenges.text: We are expanding into North Macedonia and need to register our product as certified grid-protection equipment under their national technical regulations, but our legal team has no experience with Macedonian energy law and the process has been stuck for seven months.
challenges.detail: Ulazimo na tržište Severne Makedonije i potrebno nam je da VR-400 bude sertifikovan kao oprema za zaštitu elektroenergetske mreže prema tamošnjim tehničkim propisima. Naši pravnici su iskusni u srpskom i bosanskohercegovačkom zakonodavstvu, ali makedonski regulatorni okvir ima specifičnosti koje nismo predvideli — drugačiji format tehničke dokumentacije, drugačije referentne standarde i zahtev za lokalnom laboratorijskom proverom koji nismo uspeli da razjasnimo. Proces traje već sedam meseci bez konkretnog napretka. Imamo kompletnu tehničku dokumentaciju uređaja na srpskom i engleskom, izveštaje o ispitivanjima iz akreditovane laboratorije u Beogradu i potencijalnog kupca u Severnoj Makedoniji koji čeka da sertifikacija bude završena pre nego što potpiše ugovor. Tražimo nekoga ko razume tamošnji energetski propis ili ko ima kontakte s telima koja mogu da razjasne proceduru — ne advokate opšte prakse, već ljude koji su već prošli kroz sličan proces.

challenges.text: Our field devices send telemetry over 4G but in agricultural areas signal drops cause gaps of 10–40 minutes in the measurement stream; the missing data corrupts our state-estimation results and operators lose confidence in the dashboard.
challenges.detail: Naši tereni uređaji u ruralnim i poljoprivrednim oblastima šalju telemetriju putem 4G mreže, ali signal je nestabilan i povremeno dolazi do prekida koji traju između deset i četrdeset minuta. Tokom tih pauza uređaji čuvaju podatke lokalno, ali kada se veza uspostavi, backend ih prima u nepravilnim naletima, a ne kao uredan vremenski niz. Naš modul za procenu stanja mreže pretpostavlja kontinuirane merne serije i kada naiđe na praznine, ili daje pogrešne procene ili odbija da radi dok operator ručno ne potvrdi status. Imamo bazu podataka s godinu dana takvih prekida i znamo tačno koje lokacije su najproblematičnije. Pokušali smo jednostavno linearno popunjavanje praznina, ali to nije dovoljno — kada se radi o promenljivim teretima kao što su sistemi za navodnjavanje, greška postaje prevelika. Trebaće nam metod koji uzima u obzir kontekst opterećenja i vreme dana, a može da radi u realnom vremenu čim stignu zakasneli paketi.

companies.plans: U narednih godinu dana planiramo da završimo sertifikaciju u Severnoj Makedoniji i potpišemo prve ugovore na tom tržištu, a zatim počnemo pripremu za ulazak u Albaniju. Paralelno radimo na novoj verziji VR-400 s poboljšanom otpornošću na elektromagnetne smetnje.
companies.rd_capacity: Imamo interno četiri inženjera koji rade na istraživanju i razvoju s punim radnim vremenom, s pristupom laboratorijskoj opremi za testiranje zaštitnih uređaja u NTP Novi Sad.
companies.past_collaborations: Sarađivali smo s firmom Elektromont Inženjering d.o.o. iz Beograda na terenskoj validaciji VR-400 uređaja tokom 2022. godine, bez formalne akademske saradnje do sada.

companies.name: Ekran Media Group d.o.o.
companies.sector: Marketing tech, media and creative studios
companies.about: Ekran Media Group d.o.o. has been part of everyday life in the Banat region since 1987, when our founders launched a small production studio in Zrenjanin to cover local news that larger broadcasters overlooked. Over the decades we grew into a regional media group operating Kanal 7, a full-schedule local television channel; Banat.rs, an online news portal attracting around 340 000 unique visitors each month; and an out-of-home advertising network of 48 LED panels spread across Zrenjanin, Kikinda and Pančevo. In recent years we added a programmatic display unit that delivers roughly 12 million impressions per month for advertisers who want to reach Banat audiences with measurable results. Our 210 colleagues include journalists, video editors, field technicians, ad-operations staff and software developers who maintain our in-house content management systems. Our clients range from regional retail chains and car dealerships to national fast-moving-consumer-goods brands that want a genuine foothold in smaller Serbian cities. What keeps us different from national competitors is a 35-year archive of local footage, direct relationships with municipal governments and local businesses, and the ability to run a campaign across television, outdoor and digital display from a single point of contact. We are not a flashy startup; we are a regional institution that is modernising deliberately.

Banat.rs – online news portal covering Zrenjanin, Kikinda and Pančevo
Banat Outdoor – LED out-of-home advertising network across 48 panels in three cities
Banat Programmatic – display advertising unit serving targeted inventory to regional and national buyers
Studio Ekran – video production and post-production services for commercial clients

challenges.text: Our programmatic display network serves 12 million impressions a month but our brand-safety filter blocks roughly 22 % of premium inventory because it over-classifies Serbian news articles as sensitive content; that misclassification is costing us around 9 000 EUR a month in refused bids.
challenges.detail: Our in-house brand-safety filter was built three years ago around a keyword blocklist that was originally written for English-language content and then translated manually. It checks article titles and the first paragraph before deciding whether to allow a bid. The problem is that Serbian news language is dense with words that the filter reads as sensitive — terms like 'napad', 'kriza' or 'protest' appear in perfectly normal local reporting but get flagged the same way a genuine harmful article would. Right now about 22 percent of the inventory we offer to premium buyers gets blocked at the bid-evaluation stage, which translates to roughly 9 000 EUR of refused revenue each month. We have tried expanding the whitelist by hand, but our ad-ops team of three people cannot keep pace with editorial output. We have the full article text available in our ad server at decision time, and we log every blocked impression with its URL and the keywords that triggered the block. A good outcome would be a classifier that understands Serbian-language context well enough to cut that false-positive rate to below five percent without letting genuinely harmful content through.

challenges.text: Our 48 out-of-home LED panels currently show the same playlist regardless of weather, traffic or time of day; we want dynamic content triggers but have no data pipeline connecting traffic counts or weather feeds to our CMS.
challenges.detail: Our 48 LED panels are managed through a Scala-based CMS that schedules playlists in fixed daily blocks — morning, afternoon, evening. The panels themselves are network-connected and can receive new playlist instructions within about two minutes of a push command. What we do not have is any live data feeding into that CMS. We have spoken to the municipal traffic authority in Zrenjanin about accessing their loop-detector counts but the data is available only as a daily CSV export, not a live feed. For weather we have been using a manual check by the scheduling coordinator each morning. Advertisers are increasingly asking for daypart and context-triggered buys — a hot-drinks brand wants to activate only when temperature drops below eight degrees, a petrol station wants higher frequency during morning rush. We would need a lightweight data pipeline that pulls weather and traffic signals in near-real time, applies simple trigger rules we can configure ourselves, and pushes updated playlists to the CMS. We have one developer who could maintain such a system once it is built, but we do not have the in-house capacity to design and build it from scratch.

challenges.text: We commissioned an audience-perception study two years ago, but we have no ongoing way to measure how editorial tone and topic mix on our news portal affects trust scores among different age cohorts; we're flying blind when making programming decisions.
challenges.detail: Two years ago we paid an external research agency to run a telephone survey of 600 Banat residents measuring how much they trusted Banat.rs and what topics they associated with us. The results were useful at the time but they are already dated and we have no way to refresh them without commissioning another expensive study. What we want is a method of continuously estimating audience trust and topic perception from signals we already collect — page dwell time, return visit rate, comment sentiment, share counts across our social pages, and reader letters to the editorial team. We produce roughly 40 articles a day across politics, local economy, culture, sport and emergency services. We suspect that heavy coverage of crime and municipal disputes lowers trust scores among readers over 55 while younger readers respond differently, but we have no data to confirm or challenge that. A usable outcome would be a lightweight dashboard updated weekly that shows how editorial mix and tone correlate with proxy trust indicators, broken down by at least two age cohorts. We have GA4 data going back 18 months and can export comment and social data manually for now.

challenges.text: The TV channel's archive of 35 years of local broadcasts sits on about 14 000 DV and BetaSP tapes in a climate-controlled room; digitising and indexing them is urgent but we have no budget line approved for it and the project estimate came in at 280 000 EUR.
challenges.detail: Since 1987 our camera crews have recorded every significant event in Zrenjanin and the surrounding municipalities. That footage lives on approximately 14 000 DV and BetaSP tapes stored in a dedicated climate-controlled room at our Zrenjanin facility. A specialist firm inspected the tapes last year and estimated that around 18 percent show early signs of binder degradation, meaning the window for safe playback is narrowing. The same firm quoted us 280 000 EUR for full digitisation, quality checking and basic metadata tagging, which is more than our annual capital budget. We do not have approval for that spend and it is unlikely to come in a single budget cycle. We are therefore looking for a way to prioritise which tapes to digitise first, and for a realistic digitisation workflow we could partly run in-house using equipment we purchase or lease incrementally. Beyond preservation, the archive has commercial value — historical footage licences, documentary production, municipal anniversary programming — but none of that can be exploited until the content is searchable. An indexed digital archive with even minimal descriptive metadata would let our archive coordinator, Gordana Nešić, respond to licensing enquiries that currently have to be refused.

companies.plans: Over the next two years Ekran Media Group intends to extend the Banat Outdoor network to at least 20 additional panels in Novi Bečej and Senta, and to launch a subscription tier on Banat.rs offering ad-free reading and exclusive local reporting. We are also evaluating a joint-venture arrangement with a Novi Sad production house to offer packaged TV and digital campaigns to national advertisers.
companies.rd_capacity: We have one full-time developer and one part-time data analyst who can engage with a research collaboration, primarily on integration and testing work rather than core algorithm development.
companies.past_collaborations: We ran a six-month applied project with a Subotica-based IT training centre, Infocentar Sever, in 2021 to rebuild the Banat.rs comment moderation workflow, which resulted in a deployable tool we still use today.

companies.name: SecureEdge Labs
companies.about:
SecureEdge Labs was founded in 2019 by a small group of industrial control system specialists who noticed that most cybersecurity products were built for office networks and simply did not work well in factory floors or building automation environments. We set up shop at NTP Novi Sad and have spent the years since building monitoring tools that understand the protocols that real industrial equipment actually speaks.

Today we serve a handful of manufacturers in the Vojvodina region, a district heating operator, and two commercial real estate management companies. Our customers run Modbus RTU lines, BACnet IP segments, and the assorted legacy devices that come with any real plant. They need to know when something unusual is happening on those networks, and they need that answer without shutting down production to collect training data first.

Our team is nineteen people: four security engineers who do the core research and product work, a small software group, field technicians who handle sensor deployment, and operations staff. We do not outsource our detection logic or our SOC analyst work. When a customer calls at two in the morning about a strange spike on a PLC, it is one of our own engineers who picks up.

What makes us different is narrow focus. We do not sell a platform that does everything. We sell a sensor that sits on your OT network and a monitoring service staffed by people who have read the Modbus specification more than once.
products: EdgeWatch sensor — passive network tap and protocol parser for OT environments
SOC service — 24/7 analyst monitoring with incident triage for industrial and building networks
FloorMap — lightweight asset discovery and topology visualisation for OT segments
PolicyAudit — one-time configuration review and hardening report for BACnet and Modbus deployments
tech: Zeek network analysis framework
Rust (sensor firmware and edge processing)
Python (backend pipeline and analyst tooling)
Modbus and BACnet protocol parsers (in-house)
Elasticsearch for log storage and search
Grafana for operational dashboards
MQTT for sensor telemetry transport
Custom firmware signing chain based on Ed25519

challenges.text: We need to detect unusual behaviour on Modbus and BACnet networks without labelled attack data.
challenges.detail: Our EdgeWatch sensor captures all traffic on a customer's Modbus and BACnet segments and sends parsed records to our backend. The problem is that we have almost no labelled examples of actual attacks on these networks. Real incidents are rare, customers do not want us running attack simulations on live plant, and public datasets for OT protocols are thin and often do not match what we see in the field. We have tried writing rules by hand for the most obvious cases — unexpected function codes, register writes outside normal ranges, new devices appearing on the network. That catches some things but misses slow, low-volume probing entirely. We have also looked at statistical baselining but the baselines drift with shift patterns and seasonal production changes, which generates noise our analysts cannot keep up with. What we need is a way to build detection models from unlabelled traffic that can flag genuinely unusual sequences without needing us to say in advance what an attack looks like. We have about eighteen months of raw packet logs from three customer sites, averaging around four gigabytes per day per site. We can share anonymised versions. Our constraint is that any model has to run inference on the edge sensor, which has 512 MB of RAM and a modest ARM core. We need something we can deploy within twelve months.

challenges.text: Clients ask whether our firmware signing will survive quantum computers.
challenges.detail: Our EdgeWatch firmware uses a signing chain built on Ed25519 so that sensors only run code we have authorised. Several customers have started asking pointed questions about whether this will still hold up in ten to fifteen years when practical quantum computers might exist. We are not dismissive of the concern: these are building management systems and factory controllers with expected service lives of fifteen to twenty years, and firmware update mechanisms are exactly the kind of thing that needs to remain trustworthy for the whole lifecycle. We have read the NIST post-quantum standardisation output and we understand that CRYSTALS-Dilithium is the likely replacement direction, but we have not implemented it. Our firmware is written in Rust and the signing and verification code is about two thousand lines. The constraints are real: the sensors have limited flash storage, verification has to complete in under two seconds on boot, and we cannot break compatibility with sensors already deployed in the field without a migration plan. We would like to understand the actual risk timeline more precisely, get a clear migration path mapped out, and have a tested implementation ready before we begin EU Cyber Resilience Act certification talks. Budget for this work is modest — roughly the equivalent of a short-term engineering contract.

companies.plans: Certify under the EU Cyber Resilience Act.
companies.rd_capacity: Four security engineers.
companies.past_collaborations: None.

companies.name: Senzorika Petković i sinovi preduzetnik
companies.about:
Senzorika Petković i sinovi has been building measurement equipment for farms in the Banat region since 1998, when Dragan Petković assembled his first temperature and humidity logger for a cucumber greenhouse outside Zrenjanin. Back then the wiring was thick and the boxes were metal and nothing was wireless. Over the years, his sons Miroslav and Teodor joined the workshop, and together we moved to battery-powered wireless nodes that growers can clip to a polytunnel frame or stake into an orchard row without calling an electrician.

Today we design, manufacture, and install custom microclimate sensor nodes for greenhouses and orchards. We build roughly 400 units a year, mostly by hand, in our workshop on the edge of Zrenjanin. Our clients are fruit and vegetable growers across Vojvodina — people like the Horvat family estate near Kikinda and the cooperative run by the Stojanov brothers in Opovo — who need accurate data on temperature, humidity, soil moisture, and canopy conditions without paying for industrial SCADA systems they do not need.

What makes us different is that we stay after the sale. Every node we ship comes with a maintenance contract option, and when something breaks we drive out, not just send a manual. Our team of seven knows every installation we have ever done.

We are a small, family-run operation and we do not pretend otherwise.
products: Wireless microclimate sensor nodes for greenhouses and open-field orchards
Custom sensor enclosures and mounting hardware for polytunnel installations
Hardware maintenance and calibration contracts
On-site installation and network commissioning service
Data logging gateway units with local SD-card backup

Semtech SX1276 transceiver modules
ATmega328P and STM32L0 microcontrollers
Hand-soldering and reflow oven assembly

challenges.text: Our sensor nodes transmit over LoRa and we are seeing packet loss rates of up to 40% on parcels where the farm has metal-framed poly-tunnels — the signal reflection and multipath interference is killing reliability and clients are calling us every other week.
challenges.detail: We deploy nodes in polytunnels where the frames are galvanised steel tubing every two metres. The LoRa signal bounces off all that metal and by the time packets reach the gateway, we are losing up to four in ten. We have tried moving gateways closer, changing spreading factors, and pointing antennas at different angles, but we do not have a systematic way to measure what is actually happening at each node location before we finalise the installation. We have packet-loss logs from about a dozen affected farms going back eighteen months — that data is sitting on our server. We do not have a radio engineer on staff. We tried buying a better antenna from a catalogue supplier in Budapest but it helped on one farm and made things worse on another. Clients phone us when their dashboard goes blank and we end up driving forty kilometres for something that might be a configuration fix. A good outcome would be a practical installation guideline — antenna placement rules, spreading-factor settings — that our technicians can follow without needing a radio lab.

challenges.text: We produce about 400 nodes per year by hand-soldering and we have no quality control step after assembly — roughly 6% of units come back under warranty within the first three months, which is eating our margin and our reputation.
challenges.detail: We solder every board by hand, two people working on a batch at a time. When volume picked up three years ago we added a second reflow oven for the SMD parts but the through-hole components and final assembly are still manual. We track warranty returns in a spreadsheet and we can see that about 24 units out of every 400 come back in the first three months — usually a cold solder joint, a loose connector, or a sensor that reads out of range from day one. We do a quick visual check before boxing but we have no functional test jig. The returns cost us parts, labour, and a technician visit each time, and growers talk to each other so the reputation damage is real. We have the schematics and firmware for all our current node variants. Budget for a proper fix is limited — we are not going to buy an automated test line — but we could invest in a test jig or a simple protocol if someone helped us design it. We want to get that return rate below two percent.

challenges.text: We want to expand into Hungary and Romania but we have no CE documentation for our sensor enclosures and we have no idea what the process or the cost looks like — it has been sitting on the to-do list for two years.
challenges.detail: We have two growers in southern Hungary and one just across the border in Romania who have asked us to supply and install nodes. We quoted them, they liked the price, but then the question of CE marking came up and we had to say we were not sure. Our enclosures are custom — we machine the lids ourselves and buy the polycarbonate shells from a supplier in Novi Sad — so we cannot just reuse someone else's declaration. We have looked at the RED directive online and it is not obvious which test reports we need or whether our LoRa firmware counts as a radio device that needs a notified body or whether we can self-declare. We have no contacts at a testing lab. We have been sitting on this for two years because every time we start reading the documentation we get pulled back onto installation work. A clear map of the steps, a realistic cost figure, and a contact at a lab that handles this kind of low-power radio device would let us finally move forward. The Hungarian grower checks in with us every few months.

companies.plans: We want to supply and service farms in southern Hungary and western Romania within the next two to three years, starting with growers we already have contact with. To do that we need CE documentation in place and a more reliable product leaving our workshop.
companies.rd_capacity: We have one technically capable person, Miroslav Petković, who can spend roughly one day per week on development or testing work alongside his regular installation duties.
companies.past_collaborations: We worked informally with an electronics teacher at a secondary technical school in Zrenjanin, Branko Dević, who helped us rewrite our gateway firmware about four years ago, but we have had no formal research or institutional partnerships.

companies.name: Agroprerada Kević
companies.about: Agroprerada Kević has been making preserves in Sremska Mitrovica since 2003, when Dragoljub Kević and his wife Milena started cooking down their orchard surplus in a rented kitchen and selling jars at the Saturday market on Trg Svetog Dimitrija. Two decades later we are still a family business — our son Nikola manages logistics and the online shop, and we have six full-time and two seasonal employees, all from the surrounding villages. Our fruit comes from small growers we have known for years: plum orchards near Laćarak, quince gardens outside Martinci, and pepper fields in the Fruška Gora foothills. We do not use artificial preservatives or thickeners. Every batch of ajvar is roasted and peeled by hand, every jam is cooked in open copper pans and checked with a refractometer before it goes into the jar. Our customers are households who remember what home-made preserves taste like, specialty food shops in Novi Sad and Belgrade, and an increasing number of buyers through our own webshop. We are not the cheapest option on the shelf and we do not try to be. What we offer is traceability — we can tell you which field the peppers came from — and consistency, batch to batch, year to year. That consistency is something we work hard to protect, which is also why we are honest when something is not right and we are actively looking for ways to improve.

Single-fruit jams: plum, quince, apricot, sour cherry
Mixed pickled vegetables in brine (turšija assortment)
Quince cheese (membrillo-style solid preserve)
Seasonal gift sets for corporate and private orders

challenges.text: Our ajvar from this season's red peppers has a noticeably bitter aftertaste that we can't explain — the pepper variety is the same as last year, the roasting time is identical, but about 30% of customers who ordered last year are not reordering and three have mentioned the taste difference explicitly.
challenges.detail: This year's ajvar has a bitter aftertaste that was not there last season. We use the same Šorokšar red pepper variety from the same two suppliers, and we roast at the same temperature and time as always. The bitterness is not overpowering but it is noticeable, especially after the jar has been open for a few days. Out of roughly 280 customers who ordered ajvar last autumn, about 85 have not placed a repeat order this cycle, and three wrote to us directly mentioning the taste. We have tried extending the peeling step to remove more of the charred skin, and we tested one batch with a shorter roasting time, but neither fixed it. We do not have laboratory equipment to test for specific compounds. Our guess is something changed in the peppers themselves — maybe the soil, maybe the weather during growing season — but we do not know how to check that or what to do about it in the kitchen. We need to understand the cause before next season's harvest. Budget for outside help is modest, under 500 euros, but we are open to providing pepper and finished product samples to anyone who can analyse them.

challenges.text: We produce about 4 tonnes of jam per year and our sugar use is rising — we are adding 55% w/w sugar to hit a 65 Brix final product, but customers increasingly ask for reduced-sugar versions and we do not know how to reformulate without losing gelling and shelf stability.
challenges.detail: We cook roughly four tonnes of finished jam per year, split across plum, quince, apricot and sour cherry. To reliably reach 65 Brix — which is what keeps the product shelf-stable at room temperature without added preservatives — we currently add sugar at 55 percent by weight of the raw fruit going into the pan. Customers are asking more and more for lower-sugar versions, and a few shops in Novi Sad have told us they would stock a reduced-sugar line if we had one. The problem is that when we tested a batch at around 45 percent added sugar, the jam stayed runny and went mouldy in two jars within six weeks of opening. We know that pectin levels vary by fruit and by ripeness, and that quince behaves differently from plum, but we do not know how to calculate what we would need to add or change to get a stable gel at lower Brix. We would also need to know whether a lower-Brix product could still legally carry a standard best-before date without refrigeration, or whether we would need to change our labelling. We want a clear, practical reformulation guide we can test in our own kitchen with ingredients we can actually buy locally.

challenges.text: We want to sell on a major regional online marketplace but their onboarding requires a food safety management plan and HACCP documentation that we have never written and don't know where to start.
challenges.detail: We have been invited to list our products on Pijaca Direktno, a regional online marketplace for food producers, but their supplier agreement requires a written food safety management plan and a completed HACCP table covering our main product lines. We have never written either document. We do things correctly in practice — we check temperatures, we clean and sanitise, we track batches — but none of it is written down in a way an auditor or a platform reviewer would recognise. We looked at a government template from the Serbian veterinary and food safety authority website but it was written for much larger operations and we could not map it onto what we actually do. We do not want to hire a full-time quality manager. What we need is either a ready-to-adapt template for a small preserve producer, or someone who can spend a day with us going through our process and turning it into the documents the marketplace requires. The deadline is the end of the current quarter because we want to be listed before the summer fruit season begins.

companies.plans: Over the next two years Dragoljub and Milena plan to add a reduced-sugar product line and expand the webshop to serve customers in Slovenia and Croatia. They are also considering a small on-site tasting room to support direct sales during the Fruška Gora tourism season.
companies.rd_capacity: The team can dedicate one person (Nikola Kević) roughly one day per week to testing and documentation work alongside an external collaborator, and can provide raw materials and kitchen access for small-scale trials.
companies.past_collaborations: None formal; occasional informal advice from a retired food technologist, Vera Ostojić, who lives nearby and has helped them interpret labelling regulations.

companies.name: Indigo Atelier Studio d.o.o.
companies.about:
Indigo Atelier Studio d.o.o. was started in 2019 by Marta Vujić and textile designer Petra Oláh in a rented room in Novi Sad's Liman district. The idea was straightforward: make small runs of women's ready-to-wear that are worth keeping for more than one season, sewn from fabrics sourced within a day's drive — domestic mills around Novi Sad and partners across the Hungarian border. We moved into NTP Novi Sad in 2022, which gave us stable workspace and access to people who think about problems differently than we do.

We sell directly to customers across the EU through our own webshop, with the largest markets in Germany, the Netherlands, and Austria. Each collection runs between 1,500 and 2,500 pieces. We don't do trend cycles. We release two collections a year — spring-summer and autumn-winter — and when they're gone, they're gone.

The team is fourteen people: pattern makers, a production coordinator, two marketers, a customer-care person, and the rest split between design and operations. We keep production local, which means slower lead times than fast-fashion competitors but real visibility into who is cutting and sewing each piece.

Our customers tend to find us through social content and stay because the quality holds up. We're not trying to be the cheapest option. We're trying to be the one you don't regret.

Natural and low-impact dyed woven and knit fabrics sourced from domestic and Hungarian mills
Direct-to-consumer EU webshop with EU-wide delivery

challenges.text: We launched a size-inclusive line last season and returns are running at 34% — almost all customers say the fit was wrong — which is killing our margin because return shipping from Germany or the Netherlands costs us €6–8 per parcel and we're on a 2,000-piece run.
challenges.detail: When we launched our size-inclusive range last autumn-winter season, we were genuinely pleased with the fabrics and the silhouettes. The response online was warm. Then the returns started coming in. Right now 34% of orders from that line have been sent back, and almost every return note says the same thing: the fit was off. That hurts in two ways. First, we lose the sale. Second, a return parcel from Germany or the Netherlands costs us €6 to €8 in shipping alone, before we even account for re-inspection and repackaging. On a 2,000-piece run, that adds up fast. We adjusted our size chart after the first wave of returns and sent the updated measurements to our photographer for new detail shots, but the return rate barely moved. We think the problem is in how we grade between sizes — our pattern maker has experience up to EU 44 but the extended sizes were extrapolated, not fitted on real bodies. We don't have fit models for larger sizes on our current budget, and flying samples back and forth to a specialist is slow. A good outcome for us would be a reliable way to predict fit issues before we go into production, or at minimum a tool that helps customers choose their size more accurately before they order.

challenges.text: Our Instagram and TikTok content drives traffic but we can't convert it — our webshop session-to-purchase rate is 1.2% and the EU average for fashion is around 3.5%; we've changed the layout twice and hired a photographer but nothing moved the needle.
challenges.detail: Our Instagram account has around 18,000 followers and our TikTok short-form content regularly gets between 20,000 and 80,000 views per clip. People comment, save, and share. Then they arrive on the webshop and most of them leave without buying anything. Our session-to-purchase rate sits at 1.2%. The EU fashion benchmark we've seen cited is around 3.5%, so we're well below where we should be. We've rebuilt the homepage layout twice in the last year, hired a Novi Sad-based photographer for better product imagery, and added a size guide page. None of it changed the number in any meaningful way. Our Klaviyo abandoned-cart flow recovers a small portion, but the abandonment is happening earlier — people aren't even reaching checkout. We look at GA4 data but we're not confident we're reading it correctly or asking the right questions. We don't know whether the problem is trust, pricing presentation, the size confusion discussed elsewhere, checkout friction, or something else. We have the traffic. We don't understand why it doesn't convert, and we don't have budget for a full agency engagement right now.

challenges.text: We want to market our fabrics as 'low environmental impact' but a German wholesale buyer is now asking for a full life-cycle assessment document before they'll list us — we have no idea how to produce one and can't afford a consultancy that quoted us €12,000 for the study.
challenges.detail: A wholesale buyer at a mid-size German retailer called Feldweg Concept Store asked us, before they'll add us to their catalogue, to supply a life-cycle assessment for our core fabric lines — something that quantifies carbon, water use, and chemical inputs from fibre through to finished garment. We understand why they're asking. Their own customers are pushing for it and there's increasing regulatory movement in that direction across the EU. Our fabrics come from two mills we trust and have visited, and we know they use low-impact dyes and don't use certain chemical finishes. But we have no formal documentation of any of this. We approached one environmental consultancy in Novi Sad and one in Belgrade; the Belgrade firm quoted us €12,000 for a full LCA study, which is not something we can absorb this year. We have basic data sheets from our mill partners — fibre origin, dye class, some water consumption figures — but nothing structured. Feldweg has given us an informal deadline of end of Q3 2024 to provide something credible, or they'll move to another supplier. A good outcome is a document or methodology we can stand behind and update as our supply chain changes, without paying consultancy rates we can't afford.

challenges.text: We need a seed investment round of €150,000 to fund the next two collections and a warehouse deposit, but three angel investors passed because we don't have audited financials and our bookkeeping is done in a spreadsheet by the founder's partner who has no accounting background.
challenges.detail: We need €150,000 to cover fabric and production costs for the next two collections and to pay a deposit on a small warehouse space we've identified near Rumenka, which would replace the shared storage arrangement we currently use and give us better control over dispatch times. We've had three conversations with angel investors — two from the Novi Sad startup scene and one introduced through NTP's network — and all three passed at the due-diligence stage. The feedback each time was the same: our financials aren't in order. Our bookkeeping has been handled since founding by the founder's partner, who is organised and careful but has no formal accounting background. Everything lives in Google Sheets. There are no audited statements, no proper profit-and-loss formatted to any standard an investor would recognise, and no clear separation between company and founder cash flows in earlier years. We know this is fixable, but we don't know the fastest path to fixing it in a way that would satisfy an investor rather than just tidy things up for our own use. We're not looking for someone to do the bookkeeping going forward — we can hire for that — we need to understand what the minimum credible financial package looks like and how to get there.

companies.plans: In 2025 we want to open a small physical showroom in Novi Sad to reduce returns through in-person fit appointments and to host wholesale buyers visiting from the region. We are also exploring a fabric co-sourcing arrangement with two other small Serbian labels to get better mill pricing on shared orders.
companies.rd_capacity: We have no dedicated R&D staff, but our two pattern makers and production coordinator can allocate time to structured tests or pilots if the scope is defined and doesn't pull them fully off active collection work.
companies.past_collaborations: In 2023 we worked informally with a textile technology student group at a local faculty who mapped our dye supplier's process documentation as a course project, but there was no formal agreement and the output was not taken further.

companies.name: FreshPak Solutions
companies.about: FreshPak Solutions was set up in 2012 by two former food-logistics managers, Dragan Kovačević and Marta Ilić, who kept watching Serbian berry exporters lose shipments to bad packaging. We started with a single thermoforming line in a rented hall and a list of about a dozen growers in the Fruška Gora corridor. Twelve years later we have 60 people, three production lines, and a quality lab that runs seal-strength, permeability and drop tests every day. Most of what we make ends up under raspberries, blueberries and sour cherries heading to Germany, Austria and the Netherlands. Our direct customers are packing houses and export cooperatives; we work closely with their agronomists and logistics teams to match packaging spec to cold-chain conditions. What separates us from the large Western suppliers is response time and willingness to run short customised batches. A grower can call on a Tuesday and have trial punnets by Friday. We are not the cheapest, but our reject rate at destination is consistently below two percent, which is what keeps buyers coming back. The next step for us is moving the whole lidding-film range to certified compostable materials before the retail mandates kick in.

Sealed lidding films with anti-fog and controlled-atmosphere options

challenges.text: Raspberries for Germany arrive with mould on day 9; buyers want 14 days.
challenges.detail: We ship raspberries from Serbian packing houses to buyers in Germany and the Netherlands. The berries leave Serbia in good condition — our own quality checks confirm that — but by day nine of a typical fourteen-day shelf-life window, a meaningful share of punnets show visible Botrytis mould. Buyers have started issuing penalty deductions and two accounts have threatened to switch suppliers unless we fix this before next season, which means we have roughly eight months. The punnet itself is a standard 125 g rPET shell with a heat-sealed anti-fog lidding film. We have run informal trials with two different film grades and adjusted seal pressures, but mould rates did not drop enough to matter. We suspect the issue is a combination of micro-condensation inside the punnet and an oxygen-transmission rate that is not well matched to berry respiration at 2–4 °C. We have OTR and CO₂TR instruments in the lab and can measure headspace gas composition, but we do not have the modelling background to translate those numbers into a film specification. We also have real shipment data — temperature logs, humidity logs, and destination inspection reports — from the last two seasons. Budget for trials is limited; we can fund materials and lab time but cannot afford a large external testing programme. A good result is punnets reaching day fourteen with mould incidence below one percent, confirmed in controlled simulated-transit tests.

challenges.text: Big retailers will stop taking conventional plastic lidding film by 2028; we need a compostable one that still seals.
challenges.detail: Several large German and Dutch retail chains have told their own-label produce buyers that conventional plastic lidding films will not be accepted from 2028 onward. Two of our three biggest customers are own-label suppliers for those chains, so this is not a distant regulatory issue for us — it is a commercial deadline we have to meet. We need a lidding film that is certified compostable to EN 13432 or an equivalent accepted standard, but that still seals cleanly to our existing rPET punnet tooling at the temperatures and dwell times we run today, and still provides adequate anti-fog performance and a gas-transmission profile suitable for soft fruit. We have done preliminary bench tests with two commercially available PLA-based films. Both sealed, but seal strength was about thirty percent below our current spec and one film showed visible clouding at 4 °C refrigerated storage, which buyers will not accept. We do not have the materials chemistry background to reformulate or identify better candidate polymers, and we are cautious about switching tooling or adding adhesive layers that would compromise compostability certification. We have a budget allocated for a two-year development programme and can run seal, OTR, anti-fog and composting-screen tests in-house. The output we need is a film formulation or a shortlist of available materials that passes all four criteria, backed by enough data to submit for EN 13432 certification by mid-2027.

companies.plans: Compostable range by 2028.
companies.rd_capacity: Quality lab with three technologists.
companies.past_collaborations: Tested packaging with a faculty lab in 2020.

companies.name: SolarStep preduzetnik
companies.about:
SolarStep started in 2021 when Dragan Đurić spent a weekend installing a second-hand solar kit on his father's farmhouse outside Zrenjanin and realised that most families in central Vojvodina had no one local to call for this kind of work. He registered as a sole trader, bought a van, and began visiting neighbours. By 2023 the business had grown enough to bring in his wife Milica to handle scheduling and paperwork, his brother-in-law Nenad to help on rooftops, and three more installers from the area. Today SolarStep is a family-run micro-firm of six people serving households, weekend cottages, and small agricultural holdings across the Zrenjanin, Kikinda, and Novi Bečej municipalities.

We do not take on projects we cannot finish properly. Every installation starts with a roof inspection, a look at twelve months of electricity bills if the customer has them, and an honest conversation about what a battery actually does and does not do. We source panels and inverters from a small number of distributors we trust and we stay on site until the system is commissioned and the customer understands the monitoring app. Most of our new customers come from previous customers. That is the measure we care about.
products: Residential rooftop photovoltaic installation (3 kWp – 12 kWp)
Battery storage add-on for new and existing PV systems
Grid-tie inverter supply and commissioning
Annual system health check and panel cleaning
Small agricultural holding electrification packages

challenges.text: We size battery storage by rule of thumb — usually 1.2 times the average daily consumption — and about one in five customers ends up with a system that cycles the battery too hard in summer, which degrades it faster than we promised. We need a sizing method we can actually use during a 30-minute site visit.
challenges.detail: When we size a battery we take the customer's average daily electricity use, multiply by 1.2, and pick the nearest product size. That works fine most of the year. The problem comes in July and August on farms that run irrigation pumps or cold storage. The battery ends up doing three or four full cycles a day instead of one, and after eighteen months some of them are already down to seventy percent of their original capacity. We promised ten-year life and we are not going to hit that. We have tried asking customers to shift loads to midday when the panels are producing, but that is hard to enforce and some of them simply cannot change their routines. We have a spreadsheet where we log panel count, battery size, inverter model, and the monthly kWh readings we collect during annual check-ups. We have data from about sixty completed installations going back to 2021. What we need is a simple method — something one of us can run through on a tablet during a thirty-minute site visit — that tells us whether to go up a battery size or recommend a second unit. We do not have budget for custom software development but we could afford a few months of consultancy if the output is a practical tool or a clear decision process.

challenges.text: We can't get financing to stock more than 20 panels and 4 inverters at a time; the bank wants three years of audited accounts and we only have two. Every time a big order comes in we lose two weeks waiting for supplier delivery.
challenges.detail: Our main distributor, Elkotek from Novi Sad, gives us reasonable prices but requires payment within fifteen days. The bank will extend a stock-financing line only to companies with three years of audited accounts and we completed our second audit in March 2024. Until we qualify, we keep a buffer of twenty panels and four inverters in the garage. When a farm or a larger household comes to us needing a ten-kilowatt system with storage, we have to order specially and wait two to three weeks for delivery. In the last twelve months we lost two confirmed orders that way because the customers went with a company from Novi Sad that could start the following Monday. We have looked at factoring and one invoice-finance provider quoted us rates we could not make work. We are not looking for a grant; we are looking for advice on whether there is a financing structure or a procurement approach that a business our size can actually qualify for, or whether there is a cooperative buying arrangement with other small installers in the region that would let us hold more stock collectively.

companies.plans: SolarStep intends to add agrivoltaic installations — panels mounted over polytunnel structures — as a service line by late 2025, starting with two pilot farms in the Zrenjanin municipality. The family also wants to hire a part-time bookkeeper so Milica can spend more time on customer technical follow-up.
companies.rd_capacity: We can offer a cooperating researcher access to our sixty-installation dataset, site visits with customers who have agreed to share monitoring data, and two to three hours a week of staff time for testing and feedback.
companies.past_collaborations: No formal research collaborations to date; Dragan attended a one-day energy storage workshop organised by the Chamber of Commerce in Zrenjanin in 2023.

companies.name: TalentMost d.o.o.
companies.about:
TalentMost d.o.o. was founded in Novi Sad in 2021 by a small team that had spent years watching hiring processes in Vojvodina factories and IT offices run on spreadsheets, gut feeling, and luck. We set out to build something more systematic: a platform that reads what a vacancy actually demands, reads what a candidate can actually do, and puts the two together without the usual noise.

Today we serve around forty employers across northern Serbia, with a growing number of clients in Germany and Austria who need to fill roles in their Serbian-owned subsidiaries or remote teams. Our customers include mid-size manufacturers, logistics operators, and software houses. They use TalentMost to screen applicants, run structured interviews with automatically scored response guides, and compare candidates on a common competency scale.

Our team of nineteen works out of the Science and Technology Park in Novi Sad. Most of us came from software development or industrial HR consulting backgrounds. We deliberately kept the product narrow and practical rather than trying to cover every corner of talent management. What we do, we try to do reliably. We are currently expanding our assessment tooling and improving how the platform handles trades and technical roles in manufacturing. We are funded by an EBRD small-business credit line and a Serbian Innovation Fund proof-of-concept grant.

Structured interview builder with automatic scoring guides
Applicant tracking module with vacancy pipeline view

Reporting dashboard for time-to-hire and quality-of-shortlist metrics

challenges.text: Our matching algorithm ranks candidates well for software roles but performs poorly for skilled-trades positions like CNC operators or maintenance electricians; hiring managers in manufacturing say the top-10 lists are 'basically random' and we're losing three accounts a month over it.
challenges.detail: The matching engine was trained mostly on IT and office job data because that is what our early customers gave us. When manufacturers started using the platform for roles like CNC machine operators, press-brake setters, or maintenance electricians, the competency ontology we built did not have the right nodes. Skills like 'reads technical drawings' or 'operates Fanuc controller' just get lumped into a generic 'technical skill' bucket and the scoring collapses. We ran an internal audit last autumn and found that for software developer vacancies our top-10 hit rate against hiring-manager selection is around 71 percent; for skilled-trades roles it drops to 28 percent. We've tried manually adding trade-specific tags for a few clients, but it doesn't scale. We have annotated data from roughly 340 completed manufacturing hires we could use for retraining if someone helped us structure it properly. We need a better ontology for industrial trades and ideally a way to learn from the structured interview outcomes so the rankings improve over time. Losing three accounts a month means this needs a working prototype inside six months.

challenges.text: We want to add a short cognitive and personality screening battery to the platform, but we built the current version ourselves by copying items from free online tests; a prospective German client told us our assessment has no documented reliability or validity evidence and they won't use it.
challenges.detail: When we built the screening battery we pulled items from a mix of public-domain puzzle sets and a Creative Commons personality questionnaire. At the time we just needed something functional to demo. Now a prospect in Stuttgart, a mid-size automotive supplier, asked for a technical file showing internal consistency coefficients, test-retest data, and evidence that the scales predict job performance. We have none of that. We ran the battery on about 900 candidates over the past year and we have those response records plus eventual hire or no-hire outcomes for around 600 of them, but nobody on the team knows how to do the analysis or what standards apply. We're also not sure whether we need to rebuild from scratch or whether we can validate what we have. The Stuttgart client has given us a provisional timeline: if we can show them a basic technical report by the end of Q3 this year, the contract stays on the table. Budget for this work is limited, roughly three to five thousand euros for external support, but we can provide full anonymised dataset access.

challenges.text: We process CVs and interview recordings for candidates in Germany and Austria, which means GDPR applies, but we haven't done a Data Protection Impact Assessment and our privacy policy was written by a junior intern; if a client requests an audit we'd fail immediately.
challenges.detail: We store CV files, video interview recordings, and competency scores for candidates who applied to German and Austrian employers. That data sits on AWS servers in Frankfurt, which is good, but our internal processes have not caught up. We never completed a Data Protection Impact Assessment for the video recording feature, which is almost certainly high-risk processing under Article 35. Our privacy policy mentions 'we use your data to match you with jobs' and not much else. We have one part-time person who handles compliance alongside other admin work. A potential enterprise client in Vienna sent us a data processing questionnaire last month and we had to stall because we could not honestly answer the questions about retention periods and sub-processor agreements. We are not looking for someone to write policy documents for us; we need someone to walk through what we are actually doing, tell us where the gaps are, help us run the DPIA properly, and give us a checklist we can work through ourselves going forward. We have a budget of around two thousand euros for this and a hard deadline of before any Vienna contract is signed.

challenges.text: We need to hire a senior backend engineer with experience in vector databases to rebuild our matching engine, but we've been advertising the position for four months and every shortlisted candidate has dropped out when a Frankfurt or Vienna company matched their salary expectation.
challenges.detail: Our current matching engine uses pgvector inside PostgreSQL, which was fine at ten thousand candidate profiles. At 140 000 profiles query latency is becoming a problem and we want to move to a purpose-built vector database and redesign the indexing layer. The person we need has to understand approximate nearest-neighbour search, know at least one dedicated vector store, and be comfortable with our Python stack. We have advertised the role since December 2023 on local job boards, LinkedIn, and through two recruiting agencies. We have reached final-round interviews with four candidates. Two accepted remote offers from companies in Germany before we could make an offer. One accepted, then withdrew after a counter-offer from a Vienna-based firm. One is still in discussion but has signalled he expects a salary we cannot match. Our current budget ceiling for the role is around 3 200 euros net per month. We are open to a part-time arrangement, a fixed-term project contract, or a collaboration with a research group that would let someone apply this work toward a thesis or publication, as long as production code is part of the output.

companies.plans: Over the next twelve months TalentMost intends to reach one hundred active employer accounts in the DACH region and launch a validated version of the screening battery that meets the documentation standards expected by enterprise HR buyers. We are also preparing a seed funding round targeting Serbian and Austrian early-stage investors to support a second engineering hire and localisation of the platform interface into German.
companies.rd_capacity: We can dedicate one mid-level backend developer and our CTO, Dragan Petković, at roughly 30 percent of his time, to support any collaborative research or development work.
companies.past_collaborations: In 2022 we completed a six-month product feedback collaboration with the Vojvodina Employers' Association under a Serbian Innovation Fund voucher scheme, which gave us structured input from eleven manufacturers on competency frameworks for industrial roles.

companies.name: NeuroStep Solutions d.o.o.
companies.about: NeuroStep Solutions was founded in 2009 by a small team of biomedical engineers and physiotherapists who believed that objective movement data should be at the centre of every rehabilitation decision. Based at the Science and Technology Park in Novi Sad, we design and manufacture sensor-based gait analysis systems used daily by neurological and orthopaedic rehabilitation teams across Serbia, Croatia and Slovenia. Our StrideSense insole system and accompanying RehabTrack software platform give clinicians quantified, repeatable measurements that complement their clinical judgement rather than replace it. Today our 51-person team covers hardware design, embedded firmware, clinical software development and direct field support. We work closely with rehabilitation centres such as the Specijalna bolnica for neurological rehabilitation in Sremska Kamenica and the Ortopedska klinika Sv. Katarina in Zabok. What sets us apart is the combination of in-house sensor manufacturing, on-site clinical training and software that was built from the start around the real conditions of busy rehabilitation wards — not laboratory settings. We are not a startup looking for a first customer; we are a mature product company looking for the right technical partners to help us solve problems that matter to patients recovering from stroke, hip replacement and spinal injury.

challenges.text: Our insole pressure sensors drift by up to 8% over a six-month period in daily clinical use; we recalibrate them manually every three months at a service cost of about €180 per pair, and clients are starting to complain that the calibration windows are too infrequent between visits.
challenges.detail: Our insole sensors use capacitive pressure cells that slowly drift as the polymer layers age and compress under repeated clinical use. Over a six-month period we consistently see drift of up to 8% across a sensor pair, which is enough to throw off pressure distribution readings in a meaningful way for post-surgical patients. Right now our service team drives out to each clinic every three months to run a manual calibration routine against a reference plate — that costs us roughly €180 per insole pair per visit in labour and travel, and we have about 60 pairs deployed across 14 sites. Clients have started to flag that three months between calibrations is too long; a few have noticed readings that look suspicious mid-cycle. We have tried logging raw sensor baseline values over time to see if we can predict drift from the data, and we have a 14-month archive of baseline logs from eight deployed pairs. What we want is an on-device or server-side method that can detect drift earlier and either correct it automatically or flag it before it affects a report. Ideally we would reduce service visits to twice a year without reducing data quality. The total budget we can allocate to this is around €25 000 over 12 months.

challenges.text: We want to classify a patient's gait pattern into one of seven rehabilitation progress categories using data from 16 sensor channels at 100 Hz, but our current decision-tree model needs a 90-second walking trial to reach acceptable accuracy; clinicians want a result from a 20-second walk.
challenges.detail: The core clinical value of our StrideSense system is a classification of where a patient sits across seven rehabilitation progress categories — from early compensatory gait through to near-normal symmetrical walking. We get 16 channels of pressure data at 100 Hz from each insole pair, and our current decision-tree model was trained on trials of 90 seconds or longer. At that length it achieves around 84% classification accuracy on our internal validation set, which clinicians find useful. The problem is that many patients, especially those recovering from stroke or with significant fatigue, cannot walk continuously for 90 seconds in the early stages of rehabilitation. Clinicians want a reliable classification from a 20-second walk. When we simply apply our existing model to a 20-second window the accuracy drops to around 61%, which is not good enough to put in a clinical report. We have a labelled dataset of approximately 2 400 trials from real patients collected over five years, including 20-second segments with physiotherapist-assigned ground-truth category labels. We have tried feature engineering on shorter windows but have not had the machine-learning depth in-house to go further. A good outcome would be a model that reaches at least 80% accuracy on 20-second trials without requiring hardware changes.

challenges.text: Three rehabilitation hospitals in Slovenia are asking us to integrate with their Dedalus electronic health record system via HL7 FHIR, but none of our three developers has worked with FHIR before and the integration project has already slipped by four months while we look for a consultant who knows both the standard and Serbian healthcare data conventions.
challenges.detail: Three rehabilitation hospitals in Slovenia — all within our existing customer base — are moving their patient records onto the Dedalus system and have asked us to feed gait session data directly into their electronic health records using the HL7 FHIR R4 standard. This would remove a manual data-entry step that currently takes ward staff around 15 minutes per session and introduces transcription errors. The integration is technically straightforward in principle: we need to map our session output to the relevant FHIR Observation and DiagnosticReport resource types and stand up a FHIR-compliant REST endpoint in our RehabTrack backend. The difficulty is that none of our three developers has worked with FHIR before, and the Slovenian hospitals have specific requirements around patient identifier formats and consent flags that intersect with Serbian healthcare data conventions in ways we do not fully understand yet. We engaged one consultant who backed out after the scoping phase, and the project has now slipped four months beyond the deadline one hospital set for go-live. We have the Dedalus sandbox credentials, we have the FHIR R4 specification, and we have a clear internal API in RehabTrack that a developer could work against. A good outcome is a tested, production-ready FHIR integration delivered within five months.

challenges.text: Patients recovering from stroke show highly asymmetric gait that causes our bilateral symmetry index algorithm to output misleading progress scores — in about 30% of post-stroke cases the score actually improves on paper while the physiotherapist observes functional decline.
challenges.detail: Our SymmetryView module calculates a bilateral symmetry index by comparing step timing, pressure distribution and stance duration between left and right sides. For most orthopaedic patients this works well as a progress indicator. For post-stroke patients it frequently gives wrong signals. Stroke often produces a gait pattern where one side compensates heavily for the other, and a patient can increase their walking speed and reduce their fall risk — genuine functional improvements — while the raw symmetry index gets worse or produces an artificially good score because both sides are moving poorly in a matched way. In roughly 30% of the post-stroke cases we have reviewed with physiotherapists over the past two years, the system score moved in the opposite direction from the therapist's functional assessment. We have about 380 labelled post-stroke sessions where a treating physiotherapist recorded an independent functional rating alongside our system output. We know the bilateral symmetry index alone is not the right measure for this population, but we have not been able to build a replacement metric that the physiotherapists themselves trust and that we can explain clearly in a report. A good outcome would be an alternative algorithm or scoring approach that agrees with physiotherapist functional ratings in at least 85% of post-stroke cases and can be explained to a non-technical clinical audience.

companies.plans: Over the next two years NeuroStep Solutions intends to extend its distribution into Bosnia and Herzegovina and to launch a cloud-hosted version of RehabTrack that allows multi-site rehabilitation networks to compare anonymised patient cohort data across facilities. We are also evaluating whether a wrist-worn inertial sensor add-on for upper-limb stroke rehabilitation is a viable product extension.
companies.rd_capacity: Our internal R&D team consists of four engineers and one clinical data analyst who collectively spend roughly 40% of their working time on product development alongside their maintenance and support responsibilities.
companies.past_collaborations: Between 2018 and 2021 NeuroStep Solutions participated in a bilateral Serbia–Austria research exchange with the Fachhochschule Technikum Wien that contributed to the sensor signal processing architecture currently used in StrideSense firmware.

companies.name: MedVizion d.o.o.
companies.about:
MedVizion d.o.o. was founded in Novi Sad in 2017 by a small group of software engineers and radiologists who had grown tired of watching diagnostic backlogs pile up at understaffed hospitals across Central and Eastern Europe. We build AI-assisted imaging software that slots into existing radiology workflows without requiring hospitals to replace their hardware or retrain their entire staff.

Our flagship product, ClearFrame, analyses X-ray and CT studies and flags findings for radiologist review. It runs inside the hospital's own network, connects to standard DICOM infrastructure, and is certified as a Class IIa medical device under EU MDR. Today we work with seven hospital groups across Serbia, Slovakia, and Romania, processing roughly 11,000 studies per month.

The team is 34 people: radiologists, machine-learning engineers, regulatory specialists, and clinical integration consultants. Our medical director, Dr. Milena Horvat, trained in diagnostic radiology in Vienna before returning to Novi Sad. Our head of engineering, Aleksandar Čović, previously built imaging pipelines for a Ljubljana-based teleradiology firm.

What sets us apart is straightforward: we do not sell a black box. Every finding comes with a confidence score, a highlighted region, and a clear path for the radiologist to accept, edit, or reject it. Accountability stays with the clinician, and our software is designed to support that rather than obscure it.

challenges.text: Our bone-fracture detection model hits 91% sensitivity on our test set, but when we deploy it at partner hospitals with older Siemens and Philips scanners, sensitivity drops to around 78% — we lose about 13 percentage points just from scanner-to-scanner variation in DICOM metadata and image reconstruction kernels.
challenges.detail: ClearFrame Bone scores 91% sensitivity on our internal test set, which was built from scans collected on three mid-range Siemens and Philips machines at our main pilot site in Novi Sad. When we deploy at partner hospitals that run older scanner generations — mostly equipment installed before 2015 — sensitivity falls to around 78%. The gap comes from differences in how those scanners encode DICOM headers and apply reconstruction kernels during image processing. The resulting images look similar to the human eye but are statistically different enough to confuse our model. We have tried simple histogram normalisation and CLAHE preprocessing, and we collected roughly 1,200 additional scans from two partner sites to fine-tune on. The drop improved by about 3 points but we are still well below the 88% floor our MDR technical file commits to across deployment environments. We have a dataset of around 14,000 labelled studies in total. Our constraint is that we cannot store scans outside the hospital network, so all additional training has to happen on-site or through federated methods. We need a reliable way to close this gap before our next hospital contract renewal in Q3 2025.

challenges.text: We are trying to close a Series A round of €2.1 million with a German medtech fund, but they want a co-investor from the Western Balkans region and our local bank contacts have no experience structuring equity rounds of this size for software-as-a-medical-device companies.
challenges.detail: We are in advanced talks with Hartmann Medtech Fund, a German investor that focuses on software-as-a-medical-device companies. They have provisionally agreed to lead a €2.1 million Series A but their partnership rules require a co-investor with a presence in the Western Balkans to share deal structuring and local governance responsibilities. We have spoken to three regional banks and two small private equity contacts through the NTP network, but none of them have completed an equity round of this structure for a regulated software product before. The sticking points are the convertible note terms, the MDR-related IP valuation, and the shareholder agreement clauses around regulatory milestones. We have a term sheet draft from Hartmann, legal support from a Belgrade commercial law firm with some tech experience, and a financial model prepared by our CFO, Tatjana Lukić. The round needs to close by the end of Q1 2025 or Hartmann will reallocate the tranche. A good outcome is finding a co-investor or a financial intermediary who has already worked on at least one similar structured deal in the region.

challenges.text: Radiologists at our pilot site spend 40 minutes per shift correcting the bounding-box annotations the model generates, because our active-learning pipeline requeues the same ambiguous edge cases repeatedly instead of escalating them to a senior reviewer.
challenges.detail: Radiologists at our pilot hospital, the Radović General Clinic in Novi Sad, spend around 40 minutes per shift dealing with corrections to bounding-box annotations that ClearFrame generates. The main complaint from their lead radiologist, Dr. Jovan Petrović, is that the same difficult cases — low-contrast hairline fractures, overlapping anatomy at the shoulder and pelvis — keep reappearing in the annotation queue day after day. Our active-learning pipeline scores uncertainty per image and requeues anything below a confidence threshold, but it has no mechanism to distinguish between a case that needs more data and a case that is genuinely too ambiguous for a junior annotator to resolve. As a result, a small pool of about 200 edge cases circulates repeatedly without ever being escalated to a senior reviewer or flagged for exclusion. We have tried raising the confidence threshold, which reduced the queue size but also starved the model of useful training signal. We need a routing layer that can recognise when a case has been seen multiple times without resolution and redirect it automatically. The goal is cutting that 40-minute correction burden to under 15 minutes without reducing annotation throughput.

companies.plans: MedVizion plans to expand ClearFrame Bone into chest pathology detection by mid-2026 and to open a second clinical integration office in Bratislava to support its Slovak hospital contracts. The Series A round, if closed on schedule, will fund an engineering team expansion of six positions and a federated-learning infrastructure project across partner hospitals.
companies.rd_capacity: The engineering team dedicates approximately two days per week to research and experimentation outside of product maintenance, coordinated through a biweekly internal sprint focused on model improvement and infrastructure.
companies.past_collaborations: MedVizion completed a six-month applied research collaboration with a Novi Sad-based signal processing group through the NTP Novi Sad programme in 2021, focused on DICOM preprocessing normalisation, which produced a preprocessing module still used in the current pipeline.

companies.name: TeraRoot d.o.o.
companies.about: TeraRoot d.o.o. je osnovan 2020. godine kao spin-of projekta koji je trajao tri godine u okviru istraživačke grupe za preciznu poljoprivredu. Smešteni smo u Naučno-tehnološkom parku Novi Sad, gde je ostao i jezgro razvojnog tima. Bavimo se izradom minijaturnih sondi koje farmer umetne u zemlju jednom na početku sezone i koje zatim neprekidno mere stanje korena i dinamiku usvajanja hraniva — bez daljeg rada na terenu. Naši uređaji kombinuju elektrohemijsko merenje impendanse sa termičkim i vlažnim profilisanjem korenske zone. Trenutno radimo sa dvadesetak porodičnih i komercijalnih gazdinstava u Vojvodini, a prve probe su tokom 2023. prošle punu sezonu na kukuruzu i suncokretovim parcelama. Tim čini dvadeset dva zaposlena: hardverski inženjeri, softverski programeri, jedan agronom i nekoliko tehničara za teren. Direktor je Miroslav Kecman, koji je i koautor izvornog istraživačkog rada. Razlikujemo se od konkurencije po tome što naši senzori ostaju in situ tokom cele sezone i daju vremenski neprekinut niz podataka umesto pojedinačnih uzorkovanja. Ne prodajemo platformu sa puno opcija — prodajemo tačno onu informaciju koja govori da li koren funkcioniše onako kako treba.
