challenges.text: We're seeing surface-fatigue spalling on the output gear of our RA-40 planetary gearbox after about 9,000 operating hours — our design spec says 20,000 — and it only happens in installations where the robot makes frequent rapid direction reversals, not in continuous-duty applications.
challenges.detail: Our RA-40 planetary gearbox carries a 20,000-hour design life. In continuous-duty installations — conveyor drives, for example — we see no unusual wear. The problem shows up only where the robot reverses direction frequently, say 40 to 80 reversals per minute. In those applications we are seeing surface-fatigue spalling on the output-stage ring gear at around 9,000 hours, less than half the rated life. We have pulled failed units and measured hardness, case depth and surface finish — all within spec on the drawing. We changed the output bearing preload on one batch as a test and saw no improvement. We do not have the in-house capability to model the transient load spikes that come from rapid reversals, and we do not have a test rig that can replicate the duty cycle at accelerated speed. What we need is someone who can help us understand whether the failure is driven by contact stress during the reversal transient, by lubricant film breakdown at low sliding speeds, or by something in the geometry. A good outcome would be a design or process change we can validate on a test rig within about six months, before the next production run.

challenges.text: We machine about 1,200 actuator housings per month and our scrap rate on the final bore tolerance is running at 4.1%, up from 1.8% two years ago; we think tool wear is the root cause but we haven't been able to prove it because we don't log tool age systematically.
challenges.detail: We machine roughly 1,200 actuator housings per month and the final bore tolerance is H6 on diameters between 40 mm and 120 mm. Two years ago our scrap rate on that feature was 1.8%. It is now running at 4.1% over the last six months, which costs us in material, machining time and delivery delays. Our strong suspicion is tool wear — we use indexable boring bars and we change inserts on a fixed cycle, not on a condition basis — but we have no systematic log of insert age per spindle, so we cannot prove it statistically. We have tried tightening the replacement interval across the board, which cut scrap briefly but drove consumable costs up more than the scrap saving was worth. We have a Mitutoyo air-gauge on the final inspection station and we record every result, so we have a large dataset of bore measurements against date and machine number but not against tool identity. What we want is a way to connect the measurement data we already have to tool condition, so we can replace inserts based on actual wear state rather than a fixed schedule.

challenges.text: A large German robotics OEM has asked us to supply 4,000 units per year with PPAP documentation; we've never done PPAP before and our quality manager estimates it will take eight months just to understand what's required, which is too slow for the customer's timeline.
challenges.detail: Robotik Augsburg GmbH — a fictional German robotics OEM — has offered us a contract for 4,000 gearbox subassemblies per year starting in the second half of 2025. The condition is full PPAP documentation at level three. We have never submitted a PPAP package. Our quality manager, Dragana Vukić, has read the AIAG reference manual and her estimate is that understanding the requirements, running the capability studies, preparing the control plans and getting the first submission approved will take eight months if we work through it ourselves. The customer wants preliminary documentation in four months. We have ISO 9001 in place and we do first-article inspection routinely, so we are not starting from zero, but the specific PPAP elements — process FMEA, MSA studies, initial process capability indices — are new to us. We are not looking for someone to write the documents for us; we need structured guidance and a realistic project plan so our own team can build the competence and meet the customer's deadline.

challenges.text: Our lubricant supplier changed the base-oil formulation last year and now our sealed gearboxes are showing elevated operating temperatures — up 11°C on average — but we can't tell whether the thermal problem is in the lubricant viscosity, the seal friction, or both.
challenges.detail: Our sealed gearboxes leave the factory with a specified lubricant fill, and for years we used Termol GX-220 synthetic gear oil from our local supplier. Last year the supplier reformulated the product — same name, different base-oil blend — without a formal change notice. We only found out when a customer reported elevated temperatures. We have since measured operating temperature on twelve units in the field and eleven units on our internal run-in stand; average temperature is up 11°C compared to our historical baseline at the same load and speed. We have measured the viscosity of the new lubricant and it is slightly higher at 40°C than the old specification but within the tolerance band printed on the datasheet. We replaced the shaft seals on four test units with identical parts from a different seal supplier and saw a small reduction — about 2°C — that may or may not be significant. We do not have a way to separate the thermal contribution of lubricant churning losses from seal friction losses under controlled conditions. A good outcome is a clear answer: which factor dominates, what is the fix, and whether we need to re-qualify the gearbox thermal rating.

companies.plans: We plan to add a third machining shift by mid-2026 to support the Robotik Augsburg contract and at least one other EU customer in the pipeline. We are also evaluating investment in an in-house case-hardening furnace to reduce lead time and quality risk from outsourced heat treatment.
companies.rd_capacity: We have one senior mechanical engineer, Mihajlo Stojković, who spends roughly 30% of his time on development work, supported by two junior engineers who split their time between production support and design tasks.
companies.past_collaborations: We worked with a Novi Sad-based materials testing laboratory, Laboratorija Femur d.o.o., on a gear-steel qualification project in 2019, which resulted in a switch to a higher-cleanliness bearing-grade steel for our RA-60 and RA-80 output gears.

companies.name: Sinaps Tech d.o.o.
companies.about:
Sinaps Tech d.o.o. was founded in Subotica in 2021 by three engineers who had spent the previous decade building automation systems for mid-sized factories across Central Europe. We noticed that most affordable quality-control tools either required expensive integration work or produced so many false alerts that operators stopped trusting them within weeks. We decided to build something different: a SaaS platform that combines industrial cameras with low-cost sensor arrays and fuses the data in real time, so a production supervisor can open a browser tab and immediately see what is wrong, where, and why.

Today we have twelve people in Subotica and a small field-support presence in Hungary, where three pilot clients in the metalworking and plastic-injection sectors are running our system on live production lines. Our clients are small manufacturers with between thirty and two hundred employees — companies that cannot afford a dedicated quality engineer but cannot afford scrap rates above two percent either.

What separates us from larger vendors is that our stack runs almost entirely on hardware the client already owns: a standard industrial camera, an off-the-shelf vibration sensor, and a mid-range edge computer. No proprietary black boxes. Our team includes computer-vision engineers, a signal-processing specialist, and two people who have actually stood on factory floors and understand what operators will and will not tolerate.

Vibration-based anomaly detection module for CNC and milling equipment
Edge-deployed sensor fusion unit for camera and accelerometer data
Pilot onboarding and integration service for small manufacturers
Monthly SaaS subscription with remote monitoring and alert configuration
tech: Python and PyTorch for model training and inference
OpenCV for image acquisition and preprocessing
MEMS accelerometer arrays with custom signal-conditioning firmware
NVIDIA Jetson edge computing modules
InfluxDB for time-series sensor data storage
Grafana for client-facing dashboards
MQTT for lightweight sensor-to-edge messaging
Docker and Portainer for edge deployment and updates

challenges.text: Our vibration-based anomaly detection on CNC milling machines works well in the lab but on the factory floor ambient noise from neighbouring machines creates so many false positives that operators just switch the alerts off — we need a smarter signal-separation approach.
challenges.detail: Our vibration-based anomaly detector was trained on data recorded in a quiet test cell using a single CNC milling machine. In that setting it catches spindle wear and tool chatter with a false-positive rate below three percent. When we deployed it at our pilot site in Győr, the machine sits on a shared concrete floor next to two punch presses and a conveyor belt. The background vibration from those machines looks, to our current model, like low-level anomalies almost continuously. Operators started ignoring the alerts after about a week. We have tried a simple high-pass filter and a short-window FFT threshold, but both still let through too much floor-transmitted noise. We have roughly eight weeks of raw accelerometer logs from the Győr site — about 400 GB — plus clean lab recordings for comparison. Our signal-processing engineer can dedicate roughly half her time to this over the next three months. We are not looking for a perfect academic solution; we need something we can ship as a firmware update to an edge device with 4 GB of RAM. A good outcome is getting the false-positive rate back below five percent in a noisy multi-machine environment.

challenges.text: We want to apply for an EU Horizon EIC Accelerator grant but the application requires a certified financial audit for the last two fiscal years and we've never done one; our accountant says it will take four months and cost more than our current monthly burn.
challenges.detail: We have been shortlisted for a pre-screening call with an EIC Accelerator evaluator in October and the written application deadline is January. One hard requirement is a certified statutory audit covering fiscal years 2022 and 2023. We have clean bookkeeping — our accountant Marta Vekić has kept tidy records since day one — but we have never been through a formal audit. Two audit firms we contacted in Subotica quoted four to five months and fees between eight thousand and eleven thousand euros, which is roughly our entire monthly operating cost. We cannot delay the application because the next call opens a full year later. What we need is either a realistic path to completing a credible audit faster and at lower cost, or clarity on whether an alternative financial document — a reviewed engagement, for example — would satisfy the EIC requirement. We have all transaction records, bank statements, and tax filings readily available in digital form. A good outcome is submitting the application on time with documentation that will not be rejected at the eligibility check.

challenges.text: The camera on our quality-control unit needs to be re-calibrated every time it is moved to a new production cell, and our Hungarian pilot clients don't have technicians who can do it — each recalibration visit costs us two person-days and kills our margin.
challenges.detail: Our quality-control camera unit uses a fixed focal-length lens and a calibration target we built in-house. Getting accurate pixel-to-millimetre measurements requires a full intrinsic and extrinsic calibration every time the unit is moved to a different position on the line. This takes about three hours on-site and requires someone who understands camera geometry. Our pilot clients in Hungary have maintenance staff but no one comfortable with calibration software. That means one of our engineers drives to the site, which costs us roughly two person-days including travel. We have had six such visits in the past four months alone. We have tried a simplified single-image calibration procedure using a printed A3 target, but the reprojection error is too high for the tolerances our clients need — they are checking metal parts to plus-or-minus 0.3 millimetres. We have budget for a small hardware change if the unit cost stays below two hundred euros per device. A good outcome is a calibration workflow that a factory maintenance worker can complete in under thirty minutes using only a smartphone or a simple printed target, with no specialist knowledge required.

companies.plans: We aim to close our first paying contract outside the pilot program by the end of 2024 and use that reference to approach three additional clients in Slovakia and Austria. Securing the EIC Accelerator grant would allow us to hire two more engineers and accelerate development of automatic in-line calibration.
companies.rd_capacity: We can commit one to two engineers part-time to a structured collaboration, with full access to our sensor logs, edge hardware, and pilot-site data under a standard NDA.
companies.past_collaborations: We worked informally with a hardware prototyping workshop at a technical secondary school in Subotica during 2022 to test early sensor enclosure designs, but have no formal university or research-institute collaborations to date.

companies.name: EuroFreight Zrenjanin d.o.o.
companies.about: EuroFreight Zrenjanin d.o.o. osnovana je 1993. godine u Zrenjaninu, u vreme kada je drumski transport u Srbiji tek počinjao da se otvara prema evropskom tržištu. Počinjali smo sa dva kamiona i jednim hladnjačom; danas vozimo 28 frigorifičnih poluprikolica i upravljamo hladnjačkim magacinom površine 2.400 m² na industrijskoj zoni Zrenjanin-sever. Specijalizovani smo za temperaturno kontrolisani grupažni transport na relacijama Srbija–Mađarska–Nemačka, sa redovnim linijama iz Zrenjanina, Novog Sada i Subotice prema Budimpešti, Minhenu i Hamburgu. Klijenti su nam uglavnom proizvođači hrane i farmaceutske kompanije kojima svaki stepen Celzijusa znači razliku između isporučene i odbijene robe. Direktori operacija i prodaje rade u firmi više od petnaest godina, a prosečan staž vozača iznosi osam godina – to je nešto čime se ponosimo u sektoru u kojem je fluktuacija visoka. Nismo posrednici: sami planiramo rute, sami punimo prikolice i sami snosimo odgovornost prema klijentu. Sa 158 zaposlenih ostajemo dovoljno mali da svaki šef magacina ili dispečer razgovara direktno sa klijentom, a dovoljno veliki da garantujemo frekvenciju polazaka dva puta nedeljno na svakoj liniji.

challenges.text: Our refrigerated trailers consume about 6.2 litres of diesel per hour just for the reefer unit, regardless of outside temperature or load volume. We've heard that smarter pre-cooling and setpoint management could cut that by 20–25%, but we have no way to model or test it without risking product temperature excursions for our pharmaceutical and food clients.
challenges.detail: Svaki naš frigo agregat troši oko 6,2 litra dizela na sat bez obzira na to da li prevozimo punu prikolicu smrznutih riblje štangle za Hamburg ili pola prikolice lekova na 2–8°C za Budimpeštu. Godišnje to iznosi otprilike 310.000 litara samo za rashladne jedinice, što je blizu 40% ukupne potrošnje goriva. Čitali smo da pametno pred-hlađenje pre utovara i dinamično upravljanje setpointom mogu da smanje tu potrošnju za petinu do četvrtine, ali nismo u poziciji da eksperimentišemo dok vozimo insulinska analoga ili svež sir. Nemamo simulacioni alat kojim bismo modelovali različite scenarije punjenja i ambijentalne temperature. Probali smo da dobijemo tehničku podršku od distributera opreme, ali oni su nam ponudili samo standardni servisni ugovor. Idealno rešenje bi bila neka vrsta modela ili softvera koji bi nam rekao koji setpoint i koji raspored pred-hlađenja da primenimo za određeni tip tereta i rutu, a da ne riskujemo ekskurziju temperature.

challenges.text: Drivers on the Germany run are governed by EU Regulation 561/2006 tachograph rules, but our dispatcher still calculates driving-time compliance by hand on a spreadsheet. We've had two infringement notices in 18 months, each costing €3,200 in fines, and we're worried the next inspection will be worse.
challenges.detail: Rute Zrenjanin–Minhen ili Zrenjanin–Hamburg spadaju u najtaksi scenarije po EU Uredbi 561/2006: vozači menjaju države, uzimaju odmore na parkinzima u Austriji ili Mađarskoj, a ponekad se raspored menja u poslednji čas zbog zakašnjelog utovara. Naš dispečer Slobodan Marinković vodi sve to u Excel tabeli koja ima skoro sto redova po vozaču nedeljno. U poslednjih godinu i po dobili smo dve inspekcijske kazne ukupno 6.400 evra – obe zbog greške u obračunu kumulativnog vremena vožnje. Pokušali smo da kupimo gotov TMS softver, ali ono što smo pogledali ili košta previše za licencu ili ne podržava srpsku regulativu. Tražimo alat ili metodu koja bi dispečeru u realnom vremenu pokazala koliko ko sme još da vozi, i koja bi ga upozorila pre nego što dođe do prekršaja, ne posle.

challenges.text: About 1 in 20 of our groupage loads arrives with a cold-chain temperature excursion recorded by the datalogger, but we can't tell whether the breach happened at the shipper, at a transfer hub, or during line-haul. Without knowing where the break occurred we can't fix the process or defend ourselves in damage claims.
challenges.detail: Od svakih dvadeset grupažnih pošiljki, statistički jedna stigne sa zabeleženom temperaturnom ekskurzijom na dataloger izveštaju. Problem je što taj izveštaj pokazuje kada je temperatura izašla izvan opsega, ali ne i gde se to desilo. Naša prikolica preuzima robu od tri do pet pošiljalaca po turi, prolazi kroz cross-dock u Budimpešti i menja vozača na granici. Svaki od tih aktera ima razlog da kaže da je ekskurzija nastala kod nekog drugog. Imamo CSV datoteke sa svim merenjima na svakih pet minuta, imamo GPS podatke o poziciji vozila, i imamo dokumente o preuzimanju tereta. Ali nemamo način da sve to automatski povežemo i ukažemo na tačku u lancu gde je najverovanije nastao problem. Platili smo jednu štetu od 14.000 evra prošle godine iako smo bili uvereni da greška nije naša. Dobar ishod bi bio sistem koji nam za svaki incident generiše izveštaj sa procenom gde je ekskurzija nastala, potkrepljenu podacima.

challenges.text: We are trying to refinance the depot expansion through a Serbian development bank loan but the application requires a five-year audited cashflow projection in a format our accountant has never prepared. Two banks have already rejected the application on formal grounds.
challenges.detail: Planiramo proširenje hladnjačkog magacina za još 1.200 m² kako bismo mogli da prihvatamo sezonske viškove kapaciteta za klijente iz prehrambene industrije. Dva razvojna kredita smo već pokušali – oba su odbijena jer naša petogodišnja projekcija novčanog toka nije bila u formatu koji banka traži: trebalo je odvojeno prikazati operativni, investicioni i finansijski tok sa pretpostavkama koje su eksplicitno navedene i proverljive. Naša knjigovodstvena firma Kosović i Marković radi sa malim privrednicima i nikada nije pravila ovakav dokument. Rok za sledeću rundu prijava je septembar 2025. godine. Nemamo godišnji budžet za konsultantsku kuću, ali smo voljni da platimo razumnu cenu za konkretan, primenjiv model koji naš računovođa može da popuni i odbrani pred bankom.

companies.plans: Do kraja 2026. godine planiramo da proširimo magacinski kapacitet u Zrenjaninu i uvedemo barem jednu liniju prema zapadnoj Rumuniji. Razmatramo i postepenu zamenu najstarijih pet prikolica modelima sa efikasnijim rashladnim agregatima.
companies.rd_capacity: Nemamo interni istraživački tim, ali imamo tehničara koji prati telemetrijske podatke voznog parka i operativnog menadžera koji može da koordiniše pilot projekte uz svakodnevni posao.
companies.past_collaborations: Nismo do sada formalno sarađivali sa univerzitetima ili institutima; jedina spoljna tehnička podrška bila je kratka konsultacija sa firmom LogisTeh d.o.o. iz Novog Sada 2021. godine oko kalibracije datologera.

companies.name: Datavox Consulting d.o.o.
companies.about: Datavox Consulting was founded in 2014 by a small group of software engineers and statisticians who had spent the previous decade building reporting tools for manufacturing firms around Vojvodina. We set up at NTP Novi Sad from day one, and the park has remained our base as the team grew to 38 people. We work with companies in manufacturing, logistics, and retail distribution across Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia, and Slovenia, and we are beginning to take on clients in Germany and Austria. What we do is straightforward: we take messy operational data, build pipelines that make it reliable, and then put models or dashboards on top that help managers make faster decisions. We do not sell platforms or licences — every engagement is scoped to the client's existing systems and data maturity. Our longest-running client relationship started in 2016 with a packaging manufacturer in Inđija; they are still with us. The team includes data engineers, ML engineers, business analysts, and two project managers who handle client communication. We keep the team small enough that a senior engineer is on every project, and we avoid subcontracting core technical work. About a third of our revenue comes from retainer contracts for ongoing model monitoring and dashboard maintenance.

challenges.text: Our churn-prediction model for a telecom client tops out at 71% recall, and every percentage point we miss costs the client roughly €180,000 in lost revenue per quarter — we've tried XGBoost and basic neural nets but we're stuck.
challenges.detail: We have been running a churn-prediction model for a telecom client for about fourteen months. The model flags subscribers likely to cancel within the next 30 days so the client's retention team can call them first. Right now we are hitting 71% recall on the holdout set, and the client has worked out that each percentage point of recall we recover is worth roughly €180,000 per quarter in revenue they keep. We have tried XGBoost with extensive feature engineering — call-drop rates, recharge intervals, customer-service contacts — and we tried a straightforward feed-forward neural network, but neither moved recall past that ceiling. The training set has about 2.1 million subscriber records over 18 months, with a churn rate of around 6%, so class imbalance is a real issue. We have tried SMOTE and class-weight adjustments without much gain. The client gives us a monthly data refresh. We cannot share the raw data externally but we can work with a collaborator under NDA on anonymised samples or synthetic data. The client wants to see a meaningful recall improvement within one business quarter, and budget for this specific problem is set at around €12,000.

challenges.text: We invoice in euros but pay salaries in dinars; with the exchange rate moving 8% in six months our margin forecast was off by nearly a full point and the board is asking us to hedge, which none of us knows how to do properly.
challenges.detail: Roughly 60% of our invoices go out in euros — mainly to clients in Slovenia, Croatia, and increasingly Germany — while all 38 salaries and most local costs are in Serbian dinars. Over the first half of 2024 the EUR/RSD rate moved about 8% against us, which knocked nearly a full percentage point off our net margin compared to what we had told the board at the start of the year. We track the exposure on a spreadsheet, which is clearly not enough. The board has asked us to put a hedging policy in place before the next annual budget cycle, which is October. Nobody on our finance team has practical experience with currency forwards, options, or any structured product. We bank with two local commercial banks and we are not sure which instruments they actually offer to a company our size, or what the transaction costs look like at our volume. A good outcome is a written hedging policy we can present to the board, an understanding of which instruments are realistic for a 38-person consultancy, and ideally a connection to someone who can implement it without us needing to hire a treasury specialist.

challenges.text: Clients in Germany and Austria are now asking for a data-processing agreement and a transfer-impact assessment before they sign; our standard contract template is Serbian law and we have no one in-house who can produce the EU-compliant paperwork fast enough.
challenges.detail: Two potential clients — one logistics broker in Hamburg and one mid-size retailer in Graz — have both paused contract negotiations until we can give them a signed data-processing agreement that meets GDPR requirements and a transfer-impact assessment covering data flows from the EU to Serbia. Our current standard contract is written under Serbian law and covers data handling in a general way, but it does not address the specifics those clients need: Article 28 DPA clauses, the transfer mechanism given that Serbia does not yet have an adequacy decision, and the TIA documentation. Both clients have their own legal teams who will review whatever we send. We have a Serbian lawyer we use for general commercial matters, but she does not work in EU data law. We have looked at template libraries online but the documents are either too generic or too large-enterprise in their assumptions. The Hamburg client has indicated they could sign within three weeks of receiving acceptable paperwork. We need someone who can produce documents that will actually pass review, not just a checklist. We would consider a short fixed-fee engagement for this, somewhere in the range of €2,000 to €4,000 for the full package.

challenges.text: We have a logistics client running 14 regional warehouses and they want a real-time inventory allocation engine, but order volumes spike 4x during promotions and our current rule-based system can't rebalance fast enough — we need something that plans ahead.
challenges.detail: One of our longer-standing logistics clients operates 14 regional warehouses across Serbia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, distributing fast-moving consumer goods. They currently use a rule-based allocation system we built for them in 2021, which distributes stock according to fixed regional quotas updated weekly. The problem is promotions: when a retailer runs a campaign, order volumes at two or three of the warehouses spike by a factor of four within 48 hours, and the rule-based system cannot redistribute stock in time. The result is stockouts at the busy locations and excess at quieter ones. The client wants a system that can look at incoming orders, current stock positions across all 14 sites, and a promotional calendar, and decide in near-real-time how to reallocate. Historical order data going back three years is available, well-structured, and lives in a PostgreSQL database we already manage. The seasonal and promotional patterns are reasonably predictable — the client gives us the promotional calendar two weeks in advance. The constraint is that reallocation instructions feed into a warehouse management system that processes movements in batch windows of about 20 minutes, so true real-time is not necessary, but the planning horizon needs to be at least 48 hours out. The client has approved a budget for this project and we are targeting a working pilot before the peak November–December period.

companies.plans: Over the next 18 months we want to formalise a logistics-optimisation service line and begin taking on clients in Germany and Austria directly, rather than through local partners. We are also evaluating whether to build a lightweight SaaS monitoring product on top of the retainer work we already do.
companies.rd_capacity: We can allocate one senior ML engineer and one data engineer part-time to a collaborative research project, with access to anonymised client datasets under NDA.
companies.past_collaborations: We ran a six-month applied project with a data-engineering group at a Novi Sad technical faculty in 2021, focused on anomaly detection in time-series sensor data from a manufacturing client.

companies.name: Kovačević Finansijske Usluge preduzetnik
companies.sector: Fintech — micro-business bookkeeping and tax-filing SaaS
companies.about: Kovačević Finansijske Usluge was started in 2014 by Dragan Kovačević, a former bookkeeper, and his daughter Milica, a software developer, in their home city of Zrenjanin. The idea was simple: the paperwork burden on Serbian sole traders and micro-businesses is real, and most off-the-shelf accounting software was built for larger firms with dedicated finance staff. We built something that fits the way a small bakery owner or a freelance electrician actually works. Today roughly 1,400 paying subscribers use our web application to handle their monthly bookkeeping, VAT declarations and payroll in one place, without needing to hire a dedicated accountant for routine tasks. Our team of seven people handles everything from product development to customer support, and most of us live in Zrenjanin or the surrounding area. What sets us apart is that we have focused exclusively on the Serbian regulatory environment — the Kontni plan, the PPP-PD payroll form, the POPDV VAT form — rather than trying to adapt a foreign product. We update the tax rules ourselves when the law changes, and our customers notice. We are not the flashiest product on the market, but our churn rate is low because the software does what it promises and our support team picks up the phone.

challenges.text: About 40% of our subscribers photograph receipts instead of uploading PDFs; our current OCR misreads amounts on thermal paper about 22% of the time, which causes wrong VAT calculations and angry support tickets.
challenges.detail: Around 40 percent of our subscribers submit receipts as photos taken on a phone rather than scanned PDFs. Thermal paper receipts are the main problem — the contrast is low, the paper curls, and the print fades. Our current setup uses Tesseract with some post-processing we wrote ourselves, and it misreads the total amount or VAT amount on roughly one in five thermal receipts. That sounds manageable until you realise a wrong number flows straight into a VAT return, and then we get a support ticket, sometimes an angry phone call, and occasionally a subscriber who files an incorrect declaration with the Tax Administration. We have tried image pre-processing — grayscale conversion, adaptive thresholding, deskewing — and it helped a little but not enough. We do not have a labelled dataset of Serbian receipts large enough to train anything more sophisticated ourselves. We have budget for a short project engagement and we can contribute staff time for testing and integration. A good result would be getting the error rate below five percent on thermal paper without slowing down the upload flow for the user.

challenges.text: We want to automatically categorise expense line items to the correct Serbian account plan (Kontni plan) codes, but the free-text descriptions merchants type are inconsistent and our rule-based system requires constant manual updates.
challenges.detail: Every expense a subscriber enters has a free-text description — the merchant name, maybe a note the user typed, sometimes just whatever appeared on the receipt. We need to map each line item to the correct four-digit code in the Serbian Kontni plan so the ledger balances correctly and the annual accounts are valid. Right now we maintain a keyword lookup table: if the description contains 'gorivo' we map it to fuel, and so on. The table has about 2,000 rules and a part-time staff member spends maybe three days a month updating it when new edge cases come in from support tickets. The coverage is still poor for anything slightly unusual, and the system has no way to learn from corrections. We have eighteen months of anonymised transaction data — roughly 800,000 line items with the correct Kontni plan codes that our accountant reviewer assigned. That is the main resource we can offer. We want something that can suggest the right code with a confidence score so that low-confidence items can be flagged for human review rather than silently miscategorised.

challenges.text: Our biggest growth bottleneck is that accountants actively advise their small-business clients against self-service tools like ours — we need a channel strategy to either partner with accountants or reach clients directly without alienating them.
challenges.detail: A significant number of small-business owners in Serbia rely on a trusted accountant for everything, and many of those accountants tell their clients that self-service tools create errors and compliance risk. Some of that concern is genuine and some of it is about protecting a fee relationship. Either way, it means potential subscribers hear negative things about us before they ever see the product. We have tried running online ads, going to small-business trade fairs, and offering a two-month free trial, and while those tactics bring in some users, we keep hitting a ceiling. We are not sure whether the right move is to build a version of the product designed for accountants to use on behalf of multiple clients — turning them from competitors into resellers — or to find a direct channel that does not trigger their resistance. We do not have a sales team; this is partly a strategy question and partly a product and pricing design question. We want to grow from 1,400 to around 3,000 subscribers within two years without taking on investment that would change how we run the company.

companies.plans: Over the next twelve months we want to improve receipt recognition quality, begin testing an accountant-facing version of the dashboard, and expand coverage to micro-companies with one or two employees who currently fall just outside our sole-trader focus. We are also evaluating whether to add a basic invoicing module so subscribers can handle their full document flow in one place.
companies.rd_capacity: Milica Kovačević leads all technical work and can dedicate roughly one day per week to a collaborative project, supported by one junior developer who handles integration and testing tasks.
companies.past_collaborations: We received a small digitalisation voucher from the Zrenjanin regional development agency in 2021, which funded a third-party security audit of the application; no prior university or research collaborations.

companies.name: NebulaQ
companies.about: NebulaQ was started in early 2023 by a small group of physicists who had spent years working on quantum circuit design at research institutes across central Europe. We moved into the Science and Technology Park in Novi Sad because the cost structure made sense for a six-person company that needs to spend most of its money on compute time rather than office rent. What we do is write quantum algorithms that help pharmaceutical and biotech companies simulate molecular interactions faster than they can with classical hardware. Our first paying clients are two mid-sized drug discovery firms based in the Netherlands and one in South Korea; none of them have in-house quantum expertise, so they rely on us to translate their chemistry problems into circuits that run on today's gate-based quantum processors. Our team is four physicists and two software engineers. We are not a consulting firm that talks about quantum — we write the code, run the jobs, and hand back numbers that feed directly into our clients' existing chemistry pipelines. The thing that keeps us honest is that our clients measure us on accuracy against known benchmarks, not on how sophisticated the circuits look.

MoleculeQ Pipeline — a managed workflow service that ingests a molecular structure file and returns energy estimates
NoiseShield — a configurable error-mitigation layer that wraps any Qiskit circuit before submission

challenges.text: Error mitigation on today's noisy quantum hardware for molecular simulation.
challenges.detail: The quantum processors we use today make a lot of mistakes. When we run a molecular simulation circuit — even a fairly small one representing ten or twelve qubits — the noise introduced by the hardware pushes our energy estimates far enough off that our clients cannot use them with confidence. We have tried zero-noise extrapolation and a basic version of probabilistic error cancellation, but both approaches increase the number of circuit shots we need by a factor of ten to thirty, which drives up cloud compute costs quickly. We have about twelve months of runway, so we cannot just throw money at more shots indefinitely. What we need is a smarter mitigation strategy that keeps shot counts manageable while getting our energy estimates within chemical accuracy — roughly one and a half millihartree of the reference values we calculate with classical tools. We have clean benchmark datasets for three small molecules, a working Qiskit codebase, and four physicists who understand the problem deeply but have not found a practical solution yet. A good outcome would be a repeatable mitigation routine that runs within our existing cloud budget and passes our accuracy threshold on all three benchmark molecules.

companies.plans: Partner with a quantum hardware vendor.

companies.name: Pulmoteh d.o.o.
companies.about:
Pulmoteh d.o.o. has been building respiratory diagnostics equipment in Zrenjanin since 2013. The company was founded by Miroslav and Snežana Kovačević, who spent the previous decade servicing imported spirometry equipment for hospitals across Vojvodina and grew frustrated with long lead times and expensive spare parts from abroad. Their answer was to design and manufacture devices locally, using components sourced as much as possible from within Serbia and the broader region.

Today, Pulmoteh employs 27 people across design, assembly, calibration, and field service. Our customers include pulmonology clinics, occupational health centres, and workplace medical services in Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, North Macedonia, and Montenegro. Our flagship product, the SP-400 portable spirometer, has been placed in more than 340 clinical sites since 2017.

What distinguishes us is straightforward: we answer the phone, we stock our own spare parts, and our service technicians can reach most customers in the Western Balkans within 48 hours. We do not claim to compete on brand recognition with multinational suppliers, but our pricing, response times, and willingness to adapt device firmware or reporting formats to local regulatory requirements have built a loyal client base. The Kovačević family continues to own and manage the business, and every assembly decision is made in-house.

challenges.text: We are seeing a 15% return rate on our flagship SP-400 spirometer because the plastic turbine blades warp slightly after about 800 measurement cycles at high humidity; the deformation is under 0.3 mm but it shifts flow calibration enough to trigger out-of-spec results.
challenges.detail: The SP-400 uses a small turbine assembly with four injection-moulded polycarbonate blades to measure airflow. After roughly 800 measurement cycles in environments where relative humidity stays above 70 percent — which is common in occupational health clinics and factory medical rooms — the blades develop a measurable warp of 0.2 to 0.3 mm. That is enough to shift the flow calibration curve outside the tolerance band we guarantee, which triggers an out-of-spec flag when the device is returned for its annual service check. Our current return rate on this issue is around 15 percent of the installed SP-400 base, and each return costs us roughly €85 in labour and parts plus the cost of a loan unit. We have already tried switching blade wall thickness and adjusting the mould cooling cycle with our current plastics supplier, Vojvođanplast from Novi Sad, but the improvement was marginal. We have also tested a glass-fibre-reinforced grade of the same polymer, which reduced warping but introduced a surface roughness that affected flow readings in a different way. We have samples, measurement logs, and return-history data going back to 2019. Our target is to get the blade geometry stable to within 0.05 mm after 2,000 cycles at 80 percent humidity. We have a budget of around €15,000 for materials testing and prototyping and would need a working solution within 12 months to incorporate it into the 2026 production run.

challenges.text: Our occupational health clients want an automated report comparing a worker's spirometry trend over three years against age- and height-adjusted reference norms; right now a technician does this manually for each patient and it takes about 12 minutes per report, adding up to nearly 30 hours of labour per week.
challenges.detail: Occupational health regulations in Serbia and Bosnia require employers to track lung function trends for workers exposed to dust, fumes, or chemicals. Our clients need a report that takes a worker's spirometry readings over three or more years and shows whether their FEV1, FVC, and FEV1/FVC ratio are changing faster than expected for someone of their age, sex, and height, using accepted reference equations such as the GLI-2012 norms. Right now our PulmoTrack software stores all the raw measurement data but has no module to do this comparison automatically. A trained technician at the clinic pulls the data, opens a spreadsheet template we supply, enters the reference values by hand, and writes a short narrative summary. We have timed this process: it averages 12 minutes per patient. Across our occupational health client base, that adds up to roughly 400 reports per month, or close to 80 hours of technician time. Clients have started asking whether competitor products offer automated reporting, and two have mentioned they are evaluating alternatives. We have three years of anonymised measurement records for approximately 4,200 patients that we could use for development and testing. Our PulmoTrack application is Java-based and runs on Windows; any new module needs to fit that environment or be accessible from it. We have one in-house software developer, Dragan Ilić, who handles maintenance but does not have capacity for a project of this size. A working automated report module, validated against our existing manual outputs, within nine months is what we are looking for.

challenges.text: We assemble 200 to 300 units per month on a mixed-model line with three operators, but scheduling which variant to build on which shift is done on paper and we routinely end up with stockouts on one SKU and overstock on another, tying up roughly €40,000 in unnecessary inventory.
challenges.detail: We build four variants of the SP-400 — differing in connectivity options and mouthpiece configurations — and two variants of the SP-200, for a total of six SKUs on one mixed-model assembly line with three operators working two shifts. Production volumes run between 200 and 300 units a month depending on orders. Scheduling which variant to build on which shift is currently managed by our production coordinator, Bojana Marić, using a printed weekly plan and a whiteboard. The problem is that demand for each variant is not uniform and not easy to predict more than two weeks out, and our current approach does not account for component lead times or shared subassembly constraints well enough. In practice, we end up short on one or two SKUs almost every month while accumulating buffer stock on others. Our finance team estimates the excess inventory tied up by this imbalance averages around €40,000 at any given time. We track orders and shipments in an older version of a Serbian ERP system, MikroERP, which exports to Excel. We have 30 months of order history by SKU. We are not looking for a large enterprise software replacement; we want a scheduling or planning tool or method that our coordinator can run each week without specialised training, ideally integrated with or at least feeding from our existing Excel exports. A reasonable budget for this is €8,000 to €12,000, and we would want something usable within six months.

companies.plans: Pulmoteh intends to launch a cloud-connected variant of the SP-400 by the end of 2026, allowing clinic-side data to sync to a hosted version of PulmoTrack without manual USB export. The company is also exploring whether its device portfolio and regional distribution relationships could support entry into the Romanian market.
companies.rd_capacity: We have one embedded firmware developer and one software developer on staff, plus access to our assembly engineering team for hardware prototyping, but no dedicated research function.
companies.past_collaborations: Pulmoteh completed a one-year product testing agreement with the Department of Pulmonology at the Clinical Centre of Vojvodina in 2021, which provided clinical validation data used in the SP-400 CE marking renewal.

companies.name: Vojvođanska Energetika d.o.o.
companies.about:
Vojvođanska Energetika d.o.o. has been working in the energy services sector since 1997, when a small team of engineers from Novi Sad began offering metering and audit services to the grain-handling cooperatives and food-processing plants that make up the backbone of Vojvodina's economy. Over nearly three decades we have grown to 88 people — engineers, energy auditors, project managers, and finance staff — and we now operate as a full energy service company, meaning we design, finance, and guarantee the results of efficiency retrofits rather than simply recommending them.

Our clients are mostly mid-size industrial and agro-industrial facilities: oilseed presses, flour mills, cold-storage operators, brick manufacturers, and commercial dairy farms. We write the contracts, arrange the financing, and recover our investment through the energy savings we deliver, measured on-site over the life of each project.

What sets us apart from consulting firms is that our own money is in every project. That keeps our assessments honest. Our audit team, led by senior engineer Branislav Čović, has completed more than 130 facility audits across the region. Project director Milena Savin oversees our retrofit portfolio, which currently covers roughly 40 active contracts. We are not a technology vendor; we work with whatever equipment the data tells us is right for a given facility.

Retrofit financing with guaranteed savings contracts

Rooftop and ground-mount PV feasibility studies

Power quality analysers and sub-metering data loggers
SCADA data export and manual CSV processing pipelines
PDF-based audit report archive (130+ documents)
AutoCAD for mechanical and electrical as-built drawings
Standard IEC 62443 practices for metering data handling

challenges.text: We finance retrofits on the basis of guaranteed energy savings, but for facilities with variable production — like a sunflower-oil press that runs flat-out October to February and idles the rest of the year — our baseline model overestimates savings by 15–20% and we end up absorbing the shortfall ourselves.
challenges.detail: Our guaranteed savings contracts are built on a baseline: we measure a facility's energy use over a reference period, adjust for weather and production volume, and promise the client a fixed saving. The problem shows up with seasonal processors — a sunflower-oil press is the clearest example. That facility runs three shifts from October through February and is nearly idle the rest of the year. When we build a baseline from twelve months of meter data and then normalise it against production tonnes, our model consistently overshoots the real savings by 15 to 20 percent once the retrofit is in place. We absorb that gap ourselves under the contract terms. We have tried splitting the year into operating and idle seasons and recalibrating separately, but the idle-period consumption is so irregular — weekend runs, maintenance heating, occasional small orders — that it introduces more noise than it removes. We have about three years of hourly meter readings for this site and two others with similar patterns. A good outcome would be a normalisation method we can apply at contract-signing that keeps our savings estimate within five percent of actual over a full contract year. We need something we can explain to a client in a one-page annex.

challenges.text: We've done 130 energy audits but they all live in PDF reports; when a client asks us to compare their facility to similar ones we have to read through dozens of documents by hand. We need a structured way to extract and benchmark key performance indicators across our whole portfolio.
challenges.detail: Every audit we have done since 1997 was written up as a PDF and filed. That is 130 documents, ranging from eight pages to over sixty, covering compressed-air systems, industrial boilers, refrigeration plant, lighting, motor drives, and building envelopes across a wide range of facility types. When a prospective client asks how their energy intensity compares to similar operations, or when a project manager wants to know what savings we typically see from variable-frequency drives on refrigeration compressors, someone has to open reports one by one and copy numbers into a spreadsheet. It takes days and the results depend on whoever does the searching remembering which facilities are actually comparable. We have tried building a summary spreadsheet twice; both times it was out of date within six months because nobody had time to maintain it. What we need is a way to pull the key figures — energy intensity per tonne of product, savings by measure type, baseline consumption by end use — out of those PDFs and into something queryable, ideally something the audit team can update when a new report is filed without specialist help. Budget for this is modest; we are not looking to build a data warehouse.

challenges.text: Two large clients want us to model how adding a 500 kW rooftop PV array will interact with their existing compressed-air and refrigeration loads during peak summer demand — they specifically want to know whether they can drop a grid connection tariff band, but we don't have the simulation tools to answer that confidently.
challenges.detail: Two of our larger clients — a cold-storage and distribution facility and a packaging manufacturer — want to add rooftop PV, both around 500 kW. They are not asking us to fund the PV; they want to know whether the generation will reliably reduce their peak import enough to move them into a lower grid connection tariff band under the current distribution network operator tariff schedule. The answer depends on how the PV output interacts with their existing large loads: the cold-storage site has a bank of ammonia compressors that cycle on fifteen-minute intervals, and the packaging site has compressed-air peaks tied to shift schedules. A few percentage points difference in coincidence between peak load and peak generation determines whether the tariff reduction happens or not, and that is worth roughly 18,000 euros per year to each client. We have fifteen-minute interval meter data going back two years for both sites and we have the compressor and air-system specifications on hand. What we lack is a simulation environment that can model PV generation against a realistic load profile with that level of time resolution and then map the result onto a stepped tariff structure. We need outputs we can put in front of clients and, if needed, show to the distribution network operator.

companies.plans: Over the next two years we plan to expand our active retrofit portfolio from 40 to 65 contracts, focusing on cold-chain and food-processing clients who face rising electricity tariffs. We are also evaluating whether to offer PV co-financing as an add-on to existing efficiency contracts rather than referring clients elsewhere.
companies.rd_capacity: We have two engineers with time partially allocated to methods development — roughly one day per week each — and access to logged metering data from our active contract sites, but no dedicated research budget or laboratory space.
companies.past_collaborations: We worked with a regional vocational training centre in Zrenjanin on a short course for facility maintenance staff covering basic energy monitoring practices, but have not previously engaged with a university research group.

companies.name: Poljoelektronika Kovačević
companies.about:
Poljoelektronika Kovačević has been building measurement electronics for Vojvodina's fields since 1993, when Branimir Kovačević set up a small repair workshop on the edge of Zrenjanin. What started as fixing irrigation pump controllers for local cooperatives gradually turned into designing and assembling our own sensor hardware. Today Branimir's daughter Milica runs the engineering side while her brother Dragan handles sales and field support. We are seven people in total, and every node that leaves our workshop has been tested by hand.

Our main product is a ruggedised sensor node that measures soil moisture at two depths, soil temperature, air temperature, relative humidity, and leaf wetness. The nodes transmit over LoRa to a small base station, and readings appear in our web dashboard within minutes. We currently have around 1,200 active units deployed with irrigation cooperatives and larger family farms across Vojvodina, from Subotica down to Pančevo.

What makes us different is straightforward: we know this soil, this climate, and these farming routines. Our enclosures are designed to survive the mud, the dust, and the heat of a Pannonian summer. When something breaks in the field, Dragan drives out and fixes it the same day. We do not outsource support. Our customers have been with us for years because of that reliability, not because of a marketing campaign.

Base station and local LoRaWAN gateway unit
Web-based dashboard for real-time sensor data and irrigation alerts
Annual maintenance and field calibration service
Custom enclosure assembly for third-party sensor manufacturers (small runs)
tech: LoRa / LoRaWAN radio communication (Semtech SX1276 modules)
STM32 microcontrollers for node firmware
Capacitive soil moisture sensing (custom PCB design)

Hand-laminated polycarbonate enclosure assembly and IP67 sealing

challenges.text: Our LoRa nodes send a packet every 15 minutes, but in dense corn canopy from July onward we see 30–40% packet loss even at maximum transmission power, and farmers are missing irrigation alerts during the hottest part of the season.
challenges.detail: From roughly mid-July to the end of August, corn plants in Vojvodina reach full canopy height, sometimes above two metres, and the crop stands in dense blocks of several hectares. During that window we see 30 to 40 percent of our data packets failing to reach the base station, even when nodes are set to maximum transmit power. We have moved antennas higher on the mounting stakes, tried changing the spreading factor, and staggered transmission times to reduce collisions, but the loss rate stays stubbornly high. The problem is worst on farms where the base station sits inside the same field rather than on an elevated edge position. Those are also the farms that most need reliable irrigation alerts, because they tend to be larger. We log every failed packet with a timestamp, so we have a clear picture of when the losses happen and on which nodes. What we do not have is the radio engineering knowledge to work out whether the fix is a different antenna geometry, a mesh relay approach, a different frequency plan, or something else. Any solution has to work with hardware we can still assemble here in Zrenjanin at a cost that does not push the node price above what cooperatives will pay.

challenges.text: We are still printing single-colour labels on our enclosures with a desktop printer and laminating by hand; distributors in Austria and Germany are asking for CE-marked labelling and multilingual quick-start cards, and our current process cannot scale past 200 units a month.
challenges.detail: Right now one person spends roughly half a day per week printing product labels on a desktop colour laser printer, laminating them by hand, and folding the quick-start card we include in each box. That process works at 150 units a month but falls apart above 200. We have two distributors in Austria and one in Germany who want to stock our nodes as a local product, but they have asked us clearly that they need CE marking visibly on the enclosure, a Declaration of Conformity in the box, and a quick-start card in at least German, English, and Serbian. Our current label does not have the CE mark because we have not gone through that process, and the card is Serbian only. We understand CE marking requires us to go through electromagnetic compatibility and environmental protection testing, and we have a rough budget of around five thousand euros set aside for that process. Beyond the certification itself, we need a repeatable way to produce compliant labels and multilingual inserts in batches of 300 to 500 units without adding headcount. A good outcome is a certified product with a professional label produced at a per-unit cost we can absorb.

challenges.text: We have 11 years of sensor readings paired with manual farm-book records, but we have never done anything analytical with that archive; we believe there is a pattern linking our microclimate data to local pest pressure but we do not have the people or tools to find it.
challenges.detail: Since 2013 we have stored sensor readings from our deployed nodes in a PostgreSQL database. That is soil moisture, soil temperature, air temperature, relative humidity, and leaf wetness, logged every 15 minutes from roughly 800 to 1,200 nodes depending on the year. Alongside that, several of our long-term customers have shared their paper farm books with us, and we have digitised the key entries: spray dates, pest observations, yield estimates. We have always suspected there is a usable link between the microclimate patterns we measure and the timing of aphid pressure or fungal outbreaks in the weeks that follow, but we have never tested that properly. We have one person, Milica, who knows Python well enough to clean the data but not to build any kind of predictive model. We have no experience with machine learning tools and no budget to hire a data scientist on a salary. The archive is messy: node IDs changed when we replaced hardware, some farms have gaps of weeks, and the farm-book records use inconsistent terminology. A good outcome would be even a simple rule or threshold that a farmer could act on, confirmed with enough data that we feel confident recommending it.

companies.plans: Milica is redesigning the KV-S3 mainboard to reduce active current draw by roughly 30 percent, which would extend battery life through a full growing season without a site visit. The company also wants to add a basic mobile app for alert notifications by the end of 2025.
companies.rd_capacity: Milica Kovačević handles all firmware and backend development part-time alongside production duties, and the company has no dedicated research budget, though it can contribute field hardware and data access to any collaboration.
companies.past_collaborations: Poljoelektronika Kovačević completed a small joint testing arrangement with the Vojvodina irrigation cooperative Agrovoda Kikinda between 2019 and 2021, which provided field validation data for the KV-S2 node design.

companies.name: GenovaMed d.o.o.
companies.about:
GenovaMed d.o.o. was founded in 2019 by a small group of molecular biologists and clinical pharmacists who noticed that Serbian prescribers had almost no practical way to check whether a patient's genetics would affect how they metabolise a prescribed drug. We set up in Novi Sad's Science and Technology Park and spent our first two years validating a pharmacogenomic testing panel focused on the CYP2C19 and CYP2D6 enzyme genes — the two variants responsible for a large share of adverse drug reactions and treatment failures in everyday cardiology and psychiatry prescribing.

Today we work with private clinics and independent pharmacies across Serbia, returning genotype reports that help prescribers choose the right drug and dose from the start rather than adjusting after a bad outcome. Our laboratory is accredited under ISO 15189 and every report is reviewed by a clinical pharmacist before it leaves the building.

The team is twelve people: four in the wet lab, two in bioinformatics, two in clinical reporting, and the rest in operations, sales, and finance. We are small on purpose — we want to stay close to the samples and close to the prescribers who use our results. What makes us different is not the technology itself, which is broadly available, but the care we put into the clinical interpretation layer and the speed at which a pharmacy or clinic gets a usable answer.
products: CYP2C19 / CYP2D6 genotyping panel for clinical prescribing support
Extended metaboliser panel covering CYP2C9, VKORC1 and SLCO1B1 for anticoagulant and statin therapy
Batch genotyping service for private pharmacy chains
Clinical pharmacist result consultation (add-on to panel reports)
Anonymised population-level allele frequency reporting for clinic research files

Multiplex allele-specific PCR for targeted variant detection
Short-read next-generation sequencing on a benchtop sequencer
In-house star-allele calling pipeline (Python, Snakemake) running on cloud VMs
ISO 15189 accredited quality management system
LIMS for sample tracking and chain-of-custody documentation

Secure SFTP and web portal for result delivery to clinic partners

challenges.text: Our CYP2C19 and CYP2D6 panel works well in the lab, but we're getting allele dropout in about 3% of samples with degraded DNA — typically saliva collected at pharmacy kiosks — and we don't yet understand whether it's the extraction protocol, the PCR design, or the sample transport conditions.
challenges.detail: We run about 120 samples a week, and roughly three or four of those come back with at least one allele that we cannot confidently call — what the field calls allele dropout. It happens almost exclusively in saliva samples collected through pharmacy kiosks rather than in-clinic buccal swabs. Our suspicion is that the problem sits somewhere in a chain of three things: how the sample is collected into the stabilisation tube, how long it sits at room temperature before a courier picks it up, and whether our extraction protocol is well matched to low-input or partially degraded DNA. We have tried two different extraction kits alongside our standard Chelex method, and we have tightened the courier pickup window from 48 hours to 24 hours, but the dropout rate has not moved much below 3%. We have a freezer of the affected samples set aside and a full record of collection timestamps and courier logs. What we need is someone who can help us design a systematic experiment across those three variables and tell us which one is doing the damage, so we can fix the protocol before we expand to more pharmacy sites later this year.

challenges.text: Our bioinformatics pipeline for calling star alleles from short-read sequencing data takes 4–6 hours per batch of 24 samples on our current cloud setup, which costs us about 9 EUR per sample in compute — that's killing our margin at the price point pharmacies will pay.
challenges.detail: Our bioinformatics pipeline takes a batch of 24 samples from raw sequencing reads to a final star-allele call in roughly four to six hours. We run two batches a day on weekdays, and the cloud compute bill is working out to about 9 EUR per sample. At the price point pharmacies are willing to pay — which is genuinely constrained by what they can charge patients under Serbian out-of-pocket pricing — that compute cost alone is a serious problem before we even account for lab consumables and staff time. We wrote the pipeline ourselves in Python using Snakemake, and it works correctly; the issue is that we have not optimised it for cost or speed. We have looked briefly at spot instances to cut the hourly rate, but we have not properly profiled which steps are the bottleneck. We think alignment and the star-allele calling step are the heavy consumers, but we are not certain. A good outcome would be getting compute cost below 3 EUR per sample and ideally cutting total run time to under 90 minutes, without touching the clinical accuracy of the calls.

challenges.text: We want to explain our test results to patients in plain language through a mobile app, but our current PDF reports are written for physicians — in user testing, 7 out of 10 patients said they didn't understand what the result meant for them.
challenges.detail: Right now, when a patient's result is ready, we send a PDF to the pharmacy or clinic and they pass it along to the patient. The PDF is written for the prescriber — it lists allele names, predicted metaboliser status, and drug-specific dosing flags in clinical language. In a small round of user testing we ran last autumn with 20 patients recruited through a partner pharmacy in Novi Sad, 14 out of 20 said they could not explain in their own words what their result meant for how they should take their medication. Seven out of ten, roughly. We want to build a simple mobile app — probably a lightweight web app that works well on a phone — where a patient can enter a short code, see their result explained in plain Serbian or English, and get a clear answer to the question they actually care about, which is: does this affect any medicine I am currently taking? We have a designer on a part-time contract and we can write the clinical content ourselves. What we are missing is help structuring the information in a way that is genuinely clear to someone with no medical background, and guidance on how to test whether it actually works before we release it.

companies.plans: GenovaMed plans to expand its pharmacy channel to at least three additional cities in Serbia by the end of 2025 and to launch a pilot in one private clinic network in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The company is also preparing a Series A fundraising round to support wet-lab capacity expansion and the mobile patient app.
companies.rd_capacity: The two-person bioinformatics team and two senior molecular biologists can dedicate roughly two days per week each to a collaborative project, with access to the in-house sequencer, a set of retained clinical samples held under ethics approval, and a small discretionary R&D budget of approximately 8,000 EUR per year.
companies.past_collaborations: GenovaMed completed a six-month feasibility project in 2022 with a private clinical laboratory in Novi Sad, Labora Centar d.o.o., to cross-validate allele calls between the two sites' sequencing workflows.

companies.name: Datakor Consulting d.o.o.
companies.about: Datakor Consulting d.o.o. osnovan je 2014. godine u Novom Sadu, sa sedištem u Naučno-tehnološkom parku Novi Sad. Počeli smo kao tročlani tim koji je pomagao lokalnim fabrikama da razumeju šta im zapravo govore njihovi podaci. Danas nas je 34 i radimo s klijentima u prerađivačkoj industriji i logistici širom Zapadnog Balkana i Centralne Evrope. Naš posao je da iz operativnih podataka koje klijenti već imaju izgradimo nešto upotrebljivo — dashboard koji menadžer može otvoriti ujutru i odmah znati gde stoji, prediktivni model koji upozorava pre nego što dođe do zastoja, ili pipeline koji eliminiše ručno izveštavanje. Ne prodajemo gotova rešenja s police. Svaki projekat počinjemo analizom procesa na terenu, razgovaramo s ljudima koji rade sa podacima svaki dan, i tek onda pravimo arhitekturu rešenja. Tim čine inženjeri podataka, ML inženjeri i analitičari s iskustvom u automobilskoj industriji, prehrambenoj proizvodnji i transportnoj logistici. Trenutno sarađujemo s dvadesetak aktivnih klijenata, od kojih su trojica u Hrvatskoj, dvojica u Sloveniji i jedan u Severnoj Makedoniji. Razlikujemo se po tome što ostajemo uz klijenta i nakon primopredaje — pratimo performanse modela, ažuriramo ih i brinemo da zaista ostanu u upotrebi.

challenges.text: Our clients in the automotive supply chain generate time-series sensor logs at 10 ms intervals from assembly lines, and our current anomaly-detection pipeline flags roughly 22% false positives per shift, which means floor managers have started ignoring the alerts entirely — we need a fundamentally better approach to separating real drift from normal process variation.
challenges.detail: Radimo s nekoliko klijenata u automobilskom dobavnom lancu čije montažne linije šalju senzorske logove svakih 10 milisekundi. To je ogroman obim podataka, i naš trenutni sistem za detekciju anomalija — zasnovan na statičkim pragovima i jednostavnim z-score pravilima — generiše oko 22% lažnih uzbuna po smeni. Pošto se to ponavlja svaki dan, menadžeri na terenu su počeli da ignorišu upozorenja. Posledica je da prave greške prolaze nezapaženo dok ne postanu skupi problem. Probali smo da ručno podešavamo pragove po liniji, ali procesi variraju zavisno od smene, temperature u hali i tipa materijala, pa statički pragovi nikad nisu dovoljno precizni. Imamo istorijske logove za poslednjih 18 meseci i znamo koji su alarmi bili lažni — tu labelu smo prikupili ručno od tehničara. Budžet za rešenje ovog problema je otvoren ako vidimo konkretan plan, a cilj je da lažne uzbune svedemo ispod 5% bez povećanja broja propuštenih stvarnih grešaka.

challenges.text: We landed a contract with a Slovenian logistics operator worth €280,000 annually, but the deal requires us to demonstrate GDPR-compliant data residency and an ISO/IEC 27001 certification within six months — we have no in-house legal or compliance staff and every external firm we approached quoted over €40,000 just for the gap analysis.
challenges.detail: Potpisali smo ugovor s logističkim operaterom iz Slovenije — firma se zove Velox Spedition d.o.o. — vredan 280.000 evra godišnje. Uslov ugovora je da u roku od šest meseci demonstriramo GDPR-usklađeno čuvanje podataka na teritoriji EU i da dobijemo ISO/IEC 27001 sertifikat. Nemamo ni pravnika ni osobu zaduženu za compliance unutar firme. Kontaktirali smo tri spoljne konsultantske kuće — jednu iz Beograda i dve iz Zagreba — i sve tri su ponudile cenu iznad 40.000 evra samo za analizu raskoraka između naše trenutne prakse i standarda. To je za nas previsoko s obzirom na rok i na to da još nismo naplatili ni prvu fakturu od novog klijenta. Imamo dokumentovane interne procedure, koristimo cloud infrastrukturu kod jednog evropskog provajdera, i voleli bismo da nekome damo pristup toj dokumentaciji i tehničkim sistemima kako bismo zajedno napravili plan koji možemo izvesti ispod 20.000 evra ukupno.

challenges.text: About 60% of our project hours are spent cleaning and reconciling data from clients who deliver Excel files in 15 different formats with mixed date conventions, inconsistent unit labelling and duplicate rows — we estimate we lose €120,000 a year in billable capacity just on this pre-processing step.
challenges.detail: Većina naših klijenata dostavlja podatke u Excel fajlovima. Na papiru to zvuči jednostavno, ali u praksi svaki klijent ima svoje konvencije: datumi su nekad DD.MM.YYYY, nekad MM/DD/YY, nekad samo naziv meseca na srpskom ili engleskom. Jedinice za masu, dužinu i vreme nisu označene konzistentno ili uopšte nisu označene. Dupli redovi su česti jer se izveštaji prave ručnim kopiranjem iz više izvora. Imamo pet klijenata koji redovno šalju fajlove u 15 različitih formata i struktura, a novi projekti donose nove varijante. Naši inženjeri podataka troše otprilike 60% radnog vremena na ovo pre nego što uopšte počnu analizu. Procenili smo da to iznosi oko 120.000 evra godišnje u izgubljenoj naplatnoj kapacitetu. Pokušali smo da napišemo skriptove za svaki format posebno, ali to je neodrživo jer se formati menjaju bez najave. Cilj nam je sistem koji može da prepozna format, predloži mapiranje i zatraži potvrdu samo za nejasne slučajeve, bez potrebe da inženjer sedi pored njega.

challenges.text: Three of our largest clients are asking for natural-language interfaces so their non-technical staff can query dashboards in plain Serbian — our prototype works acceptably in English but the model makes systematic errors on Serbian business vocabulary, especially domain-specific terms from finance and procurement, and we don't have the annotated corpus to fine-tune it ourselves.
challenges.detail: Trojica naših najvećih klijenata — svi u prerađivačkoj industriji — tražili su da njihovi zaposleni koji ne razumeju tabele i SQL mogu da postavljaju pitanja dashboardu na srpskom jeziku i dobiju odgovor. Napravili smo prototip koji koristi jezički model i dobro radi na engleskim upitima. Problem nastaje čim se pojave srpski termini iz finansija i nabavke — 'trebovanje', 'nalog za isporuku', 'fakturna vrednost', 'devizni kurs na dan knjiženja' i slično. Model ili ne prepoznaje termine ili ih mapira na pogrešne kolone u bazi. Nismo imali resurse da skupimo i anotiramo sopstveni korpus srpskog poslovnog jezika. Tražili smo od klijenata da nam pomognu s prikupljanjem primera, ali to ide sporo jer nemaju ko da to uradi. Imamo oko 4.000 parova pitanje-odgovor na engleskom koje smo sami napravili, i 600 na srpskom koje su zaposleni kod klijenata uneli tokom pilota. To nije dovoljno za fine-tuning. Rok koji su klijenti postavili je kraj prvog kvartala sledeće godine.

companies.plans: U toku 2025. planiramo da proširimo tim za još četiri pozicije i da uvedemo standardizovanu onboarding proceduru za nove klijente kako bismo skratili vreme od prvog sastanka do isporuke prvog radnog modela. Takođe razmatramo razvoj sopstvenog SaaS alata za harmonizaciju podataka koji bismo mogli ponuditi manjim klijentima kao samostalan proizvod.
companies.rd_capacity: Trenutno nemamo formalizovan istraživački tim, ali dva senior ML inženjera odvajaju oko 20% radnog vremena za eksperimentalne projekte i praćenje novih metoda.
companies.past_collaborations: 2021. godine sarađivali smo s jednom regionalnom razvojnom agencijom na pilot projektu digitalizacije izveštavanja za prehrambene proizvođače u Vojvodini, bez formalne akademske saradnje do sada.

companies.name: PrintMetal 3D
companies.about: PrintMetal 3D was founded in 2018 by two mechanical engineers who spent years watching Serbian manufacturers wait weeks and pay import prices for simple metal spare parts. We set up inside NTP Novi Sad with one selective laser melting machine, a surface-finishing bench, and a straightforward idea: short-run metal parts, made locally, delivered fast. Today we run four SLM machines and a full post-processing line covering stress relief, heat treatment, shot peening, and CNC finishing. Our customers come mostly from the automotive supply chain, fluid-handling equipment makers, and a handful of mold-and-die shops that need replacement tooling before a production line goes cold. We work in 316L stainless, 17-4 PH, AlSi10Mg, and Ti-6Al-4V on request. What keeps customers coming back is not marketing — it is that we pick up the phone, we understand tolerances, and we do not oversell what powder-bed fusion can actually do. Our team of thirteen includes operators, application engineers, and a metrology technician who runs our Zeiss coordinate measuring machine. We are currently working toward AS9100 aerospace certification, which will open a segment we have been preparing for quietly since 2022.

challenges.text: Porosity in 316L parts fails customer pressure tests in about 1 of 12 builds.
challenges.detail: Roughly once every twelve builds, a batch of 316L parts comes out of the machine and fails a customer's hydrostatic or pneumatic pressure test. The failure is always subsurface porosity — gas pores or lack-of-fusion voids that the surface finish hides completely. We have tried adjusting laser power, scan speed, and hatch spacing manually, and we keep a log of every parameter set we have used over the past two years. The log now has about 340 build records with density measurements and pass/fail notes, but we have not been able to find a clean pattern that tells us in advance which builds will fail. We own an Olympus metallographic microscope and we do Archimedes density checks on coupons in every build, but coupon density does not always predict what happens in the actual part geometry. We do not have CT scanning in-house and sending parts out costs us time and money we cannot recover from small orders. A good outcome would be a reliable in-process or post-process indicator — or a parameter selection method — that gets the fail rate below one in fifty without slowing build times significantly. We have the full build logs available and could share coupon cross-sections.

challenges.text: Four printers, many small orders: we schedule builds by hand.
challenges.detail: We currently receive between eight and twenty separate customer orders per week, most of them involving two to thirty parts. Each order specifies a material, a deadline, and sometimes a preferred surface finish. We have four machines that each take between four and eighteen hours per build, and parts from different customers can often be nested together in one build if their material and parameter requirements match. Right now, one of our application engineers spends a full morning every Monday — and smaller chunks of time on Wednesday and Friday — manually matching orders, estimating fill rates in Magics, and writing a build plan in a spreadsheet. When a rush order arrives on Tuesday it often means redoing the whole week's plan. We lose machine utilization this way: our average platform fill is around 61 percent when we estimate it could be above 75 percent with better nesting decisions. We have looked at generic scheduling software but nothing accounts for the geometry-dependent nesting logic that Magics uses. A good outcome is a tool or workflow that takes our open orders as input and proposes a build sequence and nesting grouping automatically, or at least ranks combinations by estimated fill rate.
